docs.title: buildzr
docs.text:
Define your C4 software architecture in Python, then build it and explore it in an interactive browser viewer.

No install: edit a model and watch the viewer update.

  • Write architecture as code. Describe people, systems, containers and components with Python with blocks and >> relationships.
  • See it in your browser. One command, buildzr serve, builds your model and serves a viewer that you can zoom, search and link to.
  • Stay compatible. buildzr produces standard Structurizr workspaces, so other Structurizr tools can read your model.

docs.title: Try it now
docs.text:
The quickest way is the in-browser demo: edit a model and run it, with nothing to install.

To run buildzr on your machine, install uv (it finds or fetches a compatible Python) and run:

uvx buildzr serve --example

This serves a bundled example workspace and prints its address. Open it to explore the interactive viewer. You do not need a project, a model file or Node.js. If you prefer a browser tab, press Run Code on the complete Quick Start example: it runs without installing anything.

docs.title: Use buildzr with your coding agent
docs.text:
Let your coding agent model your architecture for you. The buildzr skill teaches it to write model files, build them, fix build errors, serve the viewer and answer questions about your model.

Install the skill in your project:

npx skills add amirulmenjeni/buildzr

Then ask your agent:

Use buildzr to model the architecture of this repository. Read the code, create or update
the model in workspaces/, add a system context view and a container view, build it, and
tell me how to open it with buildzr serve.

The agent builds the model and tells you how to open the viewer. See Use buildzr with AI agents for the requirements and what the agent can do.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
To write a model yourself, start a project. You need:

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • Node.js 18 or newer: when buildzr builds your model, its layout step runs on Node. Check it with node --version.
  • uv. With pip, install with pip install buildzr instead of uv add buildzr.

Create a project and install buildzr:

uv init hello-buildzr
cd hello-buildzr
uv add buildzr
mkdir workspaces

Save this model as workspaces/hello.py:

from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    user = Person('User', description='A user of the system')
    system = SoftwareSystem(
        'Web Application',
        description='Our main web application'
    )

    user >> "Uses" >> system

    StyleElements(
        on=[user],
        shape='Person'
    )

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=system,
        key='system-context',
        description='System Context View',
        auto_layout='tb'
    )

Build and serve it:

uv run buildzr serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The viewer shows your model; click a box to see its details. The Quick Start tutorial explains each step.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Model in Python. Nest elements with with, connect them with >>, group them, and extend an existing workspace. The DSL is type-hinted, so your editor can complete it.
  • Draw the views you need. System landscape, system context, container, component, dynamic and deployment views, with styles and cloud-provider themes (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Oracle Cloud).
  • Build and serve. buildzr build writes each workspace as static web pages. buildzr serve builds what changed and serves them on your machine. See Serve your workspaces.
  • Explore in the viewer. Expand and collapse boxes, search, filter by type or tag, inspect relationships, switch between light and dark themes, and share a link to one view or element.
  • Export. Save Structurizr JSON, and PlantUML, SVG or PNG files (these need Java; see Export).
  • Query your model. buildzr serve also exposes a read-only JSON Model API for scripts and CI jobs.
  • Run the examples in your browser. Every example in the documentation has a Run Code button that runs it without installing anything.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Documentation: the user guides, the command reference and the API reference.
  • Roadmap: what is planned and what is done.
  • Contributing: how to report an issue or send a change.

Found a problem? Check the issue tracker for known issues, and open one if something does not work.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
The buildzr command turns the architecture models that you write in Python into built workspaces: folders of web pages that draw your diagrams in a browser, with the model data next to them. It also serves them, so that you and other people can open them.

This page is the reference of the command: every option, its default, and every exit code. To learn the commands step by step, follow the Quick Start, then Serve your workspaces.

The command has three subcommands:

  • buildzr build runs the Python files of your workspaces folder and writes one built workspace for each workspace they create.
  • buildzr export runs one model file and writes its workspaces as Structurizr JSON, PlantUML, SVG or PNG files, for other tools and for documents.
  • buildzr serve builds what is missing or out of date, then serves every built workspace so that you can open it in a browser.

docs.title: Find the page for your task
docs.text: You want to… Read Describe your architecture in Python Quick Start and the User Guide Open your model in a browser Quick Start Serve several workspaces, on your machine or for a team Serve your workspaces Put the built workspaces on a web server you already have Hosting the built workspaces elsewhere Let scripts, CI (continuous integration) jobs, dashboards and AI assistants read your model The Model API and the recipes Write JSON, PlantUML, SVG or PNG files from a model file buildzr export and Export Keep your settings in one file buildzr.yaml Link to one box of a diagram Viewer links

docs.title: Words used on this page
docs.text: Word Meaning workspace A Workspace(...) that you write in Python. It is also what readers open: its viewer, its data and its Model API, at /<name>/ of buildzr serve. workspaces folder The folder of Python files that create your workspaces: workspaces/ unless -w or the workspaces: key of buildzr.yaml names another one. One file may create several workspaces. model file One Python file of the workspaces folder. built workspace The folder that buildzr build writes for one workspace: the viewer, the model data and a file called build.json. build output The folder that holds every built workspace, one subfolder per workspace. Default: .buildzr/build. viewer The web page inside a built workspace that draws the diagrams. A workspace built with --no-viewer has the model data only and is called a data-only workspace. modelHash A fingerprint of the model, shown as sha256: and the start of a hash. The same model always gives the same hash. Model API The part of buildzr serve that answers questions about a model as JSON (a text format for data), under /<name>/api/v1/. buildzr.yaml The optional config file of your project. It holds the workspaces folder and the build settings.

docs.title: Requirements and installation
docs.text:
You need:

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • Node.js 18 or newer on the machine that builds: buildzr build, and buildzr serve when a workspace is missing or out of date. The layout step of the build runs on Node. Check your version with node --version. Serving workspaces that are already built does not need Node.
  • The buildzr package. Installing it also installs the buildzr command.

Install the package with pip:

pip install buildzr

If your project uses uv, add the package to it instead:

uv add buildzr

docs.title: Run the command without installing it
docs.text:
uv includes a tool called uvx, so install uv first. uvx runs a command in a temporary environment, and you do not install anything into your project. Put uvx in front of each command on this page, for example uvx buildzr build.

The temporary environment contains buildzr, so your model file can import it. If your model file imports other packages, add each one with --with:

uvx --with <package> buildzr build

docs.title: How the commands find their settings
docs.text:
Each setting comes from the first of these that has it:

  1. An option on the command line.
  2. buildzr.yaml. When workspaces: is a list, the build: of a file’s entry comes before the build: of the whole file; see Choosing which files to build.
  3. The built-in default.

The tables below list every option. buildzr COMMAND --help prints the same list.

docs.title: buildzr --version
docs.text:
buildzr --version

--version prints the installed version of buildzr, as buildzr <version>, and exits with code 0. Run it to check which version a machine or a CI job uses:

$ buildzr --version
buildzr 1.0.0

The version in the output above is an example. buildzr --help lists --version next to the three subcommands.

docs.title: buildzr build
docs.text:
buildzr build [-h] [-w PATH] [--k N] [--text-color {wcag,c4}] [--no-viewer] [-c FILE] [-v] [-o DIR]

build runs every model file of the workspaces folder, each in a fresh Python process, lays out the diagrams of every workspace the files create, checks the result, and writes each one to <build output>/<name>/. It always builds every workspace; serve is the command that builds only what is out of date.

Option What it does -w PATH, --workspaces PATH The Python file or folder that creates workspaces. It takes one path, and it replaces workspaces: of buildzr.yaml, whether that is a path or a list of files and folders. The build: settings of the file still apply; the settings of a list entry do not. Default: workspaces: in buildzr.yaml, else the folder workspaces. --k N Room for a box that contains other boxes, as a multiple of the area of an empty box. Raise it if the insides of such boxes are too small to read; lower it for compact diagrams. A whole number of at least 1. Default: build.k in buildzr.yaml, else 4. See Choosing a value for --k. --text-color {wcag,c4} The text colour on boxes whose styles do not set one. wcag picks black or white, whichever contrasts more with the box, following the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). c4 uses the default C4 text colours. Default: build.text_color, else wcag. --no-viewer Build data-only workspaces: the model data without the viewer. It also applies to the entries of a workspaces: list that set viewer: true. -c FILE, --config FILE The config file. Default: buildzr.yaml, searched from the current folder upward. -v, --verbose Also show the line from the step that runs each model file. It counts the elements, relationships, views and levels of each workspace, and names a temporary folder. Errors are always shown. -o DIR, --out DIR The build output. Default: build.out, else .buildzr/build.

docs.title: Which files run
docs.text:
• With a folder, build runs every .py file in it and in its subfolders, in the order of their paths.
  • Files and folders whose name starts with _ or . are skipped, and so is __pycache__.
  • A file that creates no workspace is skipped with one line, skipped <file>: it creates no workspace.
  • Each file runs in its own Python process, in a temporary folder, so a model file that calls w.save() does not write into your project.

docs.title: The name of a built workspace
docs.text:
Each workspace is written to a folder named after the workspace, and served at the same name: Workspace('Big Bank plc') becomes big-bank-plc, at /big-bank-plc/. The rule:

  • Upper-case letters become lower case. Every character other than a to z, 0 to 9, ., _ and - becomes -.
  • Characters at the start that are not a letter or a digit are removed. The name is cut to 64 characters.
  • An empty name falls back to the name of the file without .py.
  • These names are reserved, because they would hide a file or an address of buildzr serve: api, assets, data, _buildzr, index.html, build.json and llms.txt. A workspace with one of them fails; rename it.
  • When two workspaces get the same name, build stops before it writes anything, with one error that names both workspaces and their files.
  • A model file that imports another model file also runs the with Workspace(...) blocks of that file, so it creates the same workspaces a second time. build then stops with the same error.

docs.title: When a workspace is broken
docs.text:
Before build puts a built workspace in place, it checks its data: the JSON schemas, and rules that the schemas cannot express, such as boxes inside their frames and arrows that end on the border of their boxes. What happens when a step fails depends on what is at fault:

At fault Examples What build does Exit code The workspace Its model file raises an error. The layout fails on this model. The data fails its checks. Writes a broken built workspace, which replaces the previous one, and prints a block for it. 1 The machine Node.js is missing or too old. The disk is full. Permission is denied. The build process is killed. Writes nothing: the previous built workspace stays as it was. Prints one error line. 1
  • The other workspaces are still built either way.
  • The build.json of every built workspace has status: ok, or broken. A broken one also has stage, the step that failed (model, layout or check), and errors, at most 50 errors of at most 500 characters each.
  • A built workspace that leaves out a theme, an image or a branding font has warnings, in the same form as errors. It is not broken: see Warnings. When it leaves out a theme icon that could not be fetched, it also has "incomplete": true, and the next build builds it again (see Theme Icons at Build Time).
  • After a failure at the check step, the data is kept next to build.json, so that you can look at what is wrong. After a failure at the model or layout step, there is no data: the folder holds build.json and the viewer, which shows the errors.
  • A model file that raises an error before it creates any workspace breaks the workspaces it built last time. On its first build, its broken workspace is named after the file.
  • A broken workspace is up to date like an ok one, so serve does not build the same broken model file again and again. Change the file, or use --rebuild.
  • A workspace with a reserved name fails without a broken workspace, because it cannot be written under that name.
  • Every built workspace, ok or broken, is written to a temporary folder first and then put in place in one step, so a reader never sees half of one.

The block of a broken workspace, red in a terminal:

buildzr: BROKEN: workspace billing (workspaces/billing.py) failed at the model step
    NameError: name 'ledger' is not defined
    billing.py, line 6: invoicing >> "Collects payments through" >> ledger
  this workspace is broken; the viewer says so

Serve your workspaces shows what the viewer, the list at / and the Model API show for a broken workspace.

docs.title: Removing built workspaces you no longer build
docs.text: A full build, without -w or with -w and a folder, removes a built workspace when its model file was deleted, or when its model file ran without failure in this build and no longer creates it (you renamed or removed the workspace in the file). It prints one line for each, such as removed old-name: its model file workspaces/old-name.py is gone. When workspaces: in buildzr.yaml is a list, a full build is a build without -w, and it also removes the built workspaces of a file you took off the list. A model file that failed because of the machine keeps all its previous built workspaces. Only built workspaces built from the same workspaces folder are removed: build.json records that folder, so buildzr build -w other/folder never removes the workspaces of your workspaces folder. A workspace built from a workspaces: list also records the config file of the list, so only a build of that same list removes it. A folder without a build.json that names its model file is never removed, nor is anything when you build one file with -w FILE. serve never removes anything: run buildzr build to tidy the build output.

docs.title: Choosing a value for --k
docs.text:
--k sets how much room the layout gives the inside of a box that contains other boxes, such as a software system with containers. The room for the inside is at most N times the area of an empty box; the box itself is a little larger, because it also holds its own name. build.k in buildzr.yaml sets the same value.

When you expand such a box in the viewer, its inside is drawn in that room. If the inside needs more room, it is shrunk to fit; it is never enlarged. For example, in the model examples/buildzr_models_example.py of the buildzr repository, the inside of the E-Commerce System is drawn at 23% of its full size with --k 1, 35% with 4 (the default), 50% with 9 and 68% with 16.

  • Raise the value when the inside of an expanded box is too small to read. The cost: boxes with an inside take more room on the diagram of their parent, so the whole diagram is larger, and the viewer shows it smaller when it fits it to the screen.
  • Lower the value for compact diagrams. You then zoom in to read the inside of an expanded box.
  • Once a box has all the room its inside needs, the inside is drawn at full size, and a larger value changes nothing more for that box. In the example, the Order Service container reaches full size at 9.
  • A model in which no box contains other boxes, such as the one in the Quick Start, looks the same at every value.
  • The value is a whole number of at least 1. The default is 4.

With --k 1, the containers fill a small area, and the viewer zooms in to show it. Order Service and Inventory Service, which contain components, are about the same size as the other containers.

With --k 9, Order Service and Inventory Service get room for their components, so they are more than twice as wide and as tall as the other containers, and the viewer zooms out to fit the larger diagram.

docs.title: buildzr export
docs.text:
buildzr export [-h] [-f FORMAT] [-o DIR] [--workspace NAME] [--index N] [--layout {dot,smetana}] [--pretty] FILE

export runs one model file FILE, in a fresh Python process in a temporary folder (so a model file that still calls w.save() does not write into your project and does not print a deprecation warning), and writes every workspace it creates, or the one you pick, as files. It does not use buildzr.yaml, Node.js or the viewer. A file that creates several workspaces gives one subfolder for each:

export/
  big-bank-plc/
    workspace.json              format json
    SystemContext.puml          formats plantuml, svg and png
    SystemContext.svg           format svg
    SystemContext.png           format png

The subfolder is named like a built workspace, and two workspaces of one file that would share a name get -2, -3 and so on in the order the file creates them. Files of an earlier export are overwritten, and files that this export does not write are left alone. Each file written is listed on a line wrote <path>.

Option What it does FILE The Python model file. It must exist and be a file, not a folder; use build for a folder. -f FORMAT, --format FORMAT json (one workspace.json), plantuml (one .puml file per view), svg or png (one image per view, next to its .puml file). Repeat the option to write several formats in one run. Default: json. plantuml, svg and png need pip install "buildzr[export-plantuml]" and Java 11 or newer; svg and png also need Graphviz, unless you use --layout smetana. -o DIR, --out DIR The output folder. Default: export. --workspace NAME Export only the workspace with this name. If the file creates no such workspace, or two with that name, the command says so, lists the workspaces with their numbers, and writes nothing. --index N Export only the N-th workspace the file creates, counting from 0. Use it when two workspaces share a name. It cannot be used with --workspace. --layout {dot,smetana} The PlantUML layout engine for plantuml, svg and png. dot uses Graphviz. smetana is pure Java and needs no Graphviz, with a rougher layout, and adds !pragma layout smetana to the .puml files. Default: dot. --pretty Indent the JSON with two spaces. By default the JSON is on one line, as w.save() wrote it.
  • A format that cannot work here (no jpype1, or Graphviz missing for svg and png with dot) is reported before any file is written, so the run leaves no half-finished folder.
  • A workspace without views gets workspace.json only, and a warning for each diagram format.
  • If the model file raises an error, export prints it, with the lines of your file, and writes nothing.
$ buildzr export workspaces/shop.py -f json -f svg --layout smetana -o diagrams
wrote diagrams/shop/workspace.json
wrote diagrams/shop/SystemContext.svg

docs.title: buildzr serve
docs.text:
buildzr serve [-h] [--example] [--no-build] [--rebuild] [--watch] [-c FILE] [-v] [-p PORT] [--host HOST] [--public-url URL] [--cors-origin ORIGIN] [PATH]

serve first builds what is missing or out of date, then serves every built workspace of the build output. It only reads: it answers GET and HEAD requests, and nothing can change a workspace through it.

Option What it does PATH What to serve. A workspaces folder or a model file: serve builds its workspaces when they are missing or out of date, then serves the build output. It replaces workspaces: of buildzr.yaml, as -w does for build. A folder that already holds built workspaces (it has a build.json, or subfolders that have one): serve serves it as it is, and builds nothing. Default: workspaces: in buildzr.yaml (a path or a list), else the folder workspaces. --example Serve the bundled example workspace, an online shop, instead of your own. See Try the bundled example. Cannot be combined with PATH, --no-build, --rebuild, --watch, -c or -v. --no-build Serve the build output as it is, without building. Node is then not needed. --rebuild Build every workspace again, also the ones that are up to date. --watch Keep watching the model files while serving: after each change, build what is out of date and reload the viewers that are open. A rebuild that fails keeps the last good build on screen. See Watch mode. Cannot be combined with --no-build, nor with a PATH that holds built workspaces. -c FILE, --config FILE The config file. Default: buildzr.yaml, searched from the current folder upward. -v, --verbose The same as for build. -p PORT, --port PORT The port, 1 to 65535. Default: serve.port in buildzr.yaml, else 8000. --host HOST The address to listen on. Default: serve.host in buildzr.yaml, else 127.0.0.1: only this machine can connect. To let other machines connect, pass 0.0.0.0; do this only on purpose. --public-url URL The address at which readers reach this server (http:// or https://), for example behind a proxy. The Model API builds its viewerUrl links from it. Default: serve.public_url in buildzr.yaml, else none. --cors-origin ORIGIN Let a web page from ORIGIN read the Model API from a browser (CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing). Repeat the option for more origins. There is no wildcard. Default: serve.cors_origins in buildzr.yaml, else none. The option replaces the list of the file; it does not add to it.

docs.title: Try the bundled example
docs.text:
To see the viewer before you write a model, run:

uvx buildzr serve --example

serve prints the address of the example, http://127.0.0.1:8000/example/ by default. It does not open a browser; open the address yourself. The example is an online shop with all six kinds of view (system landscape, system context, container, component, dynamic and deployment), so you can explore the viewer on a realistic diagram.

The example is hermetic: it is already built and shipped inside buildzr, so Node is not needed, and serve builds nothing.

  • It ignores the folder you run it in: buildzr.yaml is not read (even a broken one), and your workspaces folder and build output are not touched.
  • It writes nothing into the current folder. The files it serves are copied to a temporary folder, which serve removes when you stop it with Ctrl+C or a termination signal (SIGTERM).
  • -p/--port, --host, --public-url and --cors-origin work as usual, with their defaults (not the serve: section of any buildzr.yaml). The Model API of the example is at /example/api/v1/.
  • PATH, --no-build, --rebuild, -c and -v have no meaning for an example that is not built from your files, so serve refuses them with exit code 2 instead of ignoring them silently, for example buildzr: error: --example serves the bundled example, so it cannot be used with PATH.

docs.title: When a built workspace is out of date
docs.text:
A built workspace is rebuilt when its folder is missing, when it lacks a theme icon that could not be fetched ("incomplete": true in its build.json), or when its fingerprint changed. build records the fingerprint in the build.json of the workspace. It is a sha256 hash of:

  • the model file that creates the workspace,
  • every file whose name starts with _ and ends with .py in the workspaces folder and its subfolders (for a workspaces: list: in the folder of the file’s entry, or the folder that holds the listed file, and their subfolders),
  • the version of buildzr, and the structurizr/themes commit that its themes are pinned to,
  • the settings that change the output, as they are for this workspace: k, text_color and viewer, from an option, the file’s list entry or build:. Changing the k of one list entry rebuilds only the workspaces of that entry.

File dates are not used. Code that a model file imports from anywhere else is not part of the fingerprint: after you change such code, start serve with --rebuild. The themes and branding of a workspace are part of its model file.

docs.title: What serve serves
docs.text:
Address Answer /<name>/ The viewer of the workspace <name>, and its files, such as /<name>/data/index.json. /<name>/api/v1/ The Model API of the workspace. /<name>/llms.txt A short plain-text page that tells AI tools where the Model API of the workspace is. / With one workspace, a redirect (HTTP 302) to /<name>/, or to its Model API /<name>/api/v1/ when it is data-only. With several, a page that links to each one: to its viewer, or to its Model API when it is data-only. /_buildzr/v1/workspaces The list of workspaces as JSON. See Serve your workspaces.
  • When serve starts, it prints each build failure as build does, and a block for every broken workspace in the build output, also those built earlier. It serves every built workspace, broken ones included: / marks them as broken, and /_buildzr/v1/workspaces gives their status, stage and errors. If nothing can be served, it exits with code 1.
  • If a workspace must be built but Node is not installed, serve says so in one line and serves what is already built.
  • serve looks at the build output again when someone opens / or the list, and when an address names a workspace it does not know yet. A workspace that buildzr build adds in another terminal therefore appears without a restart. A workspace in the middle of being replaced is not served for that moment: its address answers 404.

docs.title: Watch mode
docs.text:
buildzr serve --watch builds and serves as serve does, then keeps watching the model files until you stop it with Ctrl+C (or a termination signal, SIGTERM). Without --watch, serve never builds again after it starts.

  • What is watched. The files that the fingerprint reads: every model file that serve builds, the files of the workspaces folder and its subfolders whose name starts with _ and ends with .py, and buildzr.yaml. A new model file in a watched folder counts too. Nothing else is watched: not data files that a model file reads, not code imported from outside the workspaces folder, not the build output, and not the files that editors write next to the one you save (.swp, ~ and .# files, __pycache__), so saving a file never starts a loop of builds.
  • When it builds. serve looks at the files every half second. After a change, it waits until the files stay the same for a moment, so a burst of writes (an editor that saves in several steps, a formatter that runs on save) gives one build of the last version. Then it builds what the change made out of date, as serve does when it starts, and prints a changed: line and the same lines as build. A file that you save without changing it builds nothing. A change made while a build runs starts another build when that one ends.
  • The viewers reload. Each viewer page of a workspace that was built again reloads by itself and keeps its address, so the same view stays open. A page asks serve once a second whether its workspace was rebuilt (a HEAD request for its build.json); only serve --watch adds this to the viewer pages, and the built files do not change. An embedded viewer whose page sends it its data does not reload.
  • A rebuild that fails keeps the last good build. If the model file raises an error, or the layout or the checks fail, the block of the broken workspace is printed with the line the last good build is still served; save a fix to rebuild. The workspace that was served stays as it was, and its viewers do not reload. When you save a fix, the next build replaces it. A workspace that was never built without errors is written broken, as serve does without --watch, and its viewers reload to show the new errors. If Node or the disk fails, nothing is written, as for build.
  • Removing. Unlike serve without --watch, a rebuild removes the built workspaces that no model file creates any more, as build does: after you delete a model file or rename a workspace in it.
  • buildzr.yaml. A change to it is not applied: serve prints buildzr.yaml changed; restart buildzr serve --watch to use its new settings. Stop serve and start it again.
  • Stopping. Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops the watch, the server and a build that is running, with the Python process that runs a model file and the Node process of the layout. A built workspace is written aside and then moved into place, so stopping never leaves a half-written one.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success. serve exits with 0 when you stop it with Ctrl+C (serve --example: also with SIGTERM). 1 A workspace is broken or could not be built, there was nothing to serve, or the port is in use. For export: the model file raised an error or creates no workspace, or the export failed (for example, Java or Graphviz is missing). 2 A usage or config error: an unknown option, an option that cannot be combined with another (such as --example with PATH), a workspaces folder or path that does not exist, an export file that does not exist, is a folder, or has no workspace of the name or number you gave, or a problem in buildzr.yaml.

Error messages from the command start with buildzr: error:. Problems in buildzr.yaml are listed one per line, as buildzr.yaml:<line>: <key>: <message>.

In the examples on these pages, a last line such as [exit code 2] shows the exit code. The command does not print that line.

docs.title: buildzr.yaml
docs.text:
buildzr.yaml is the config file of your project. It holds what the buildzr commands need besides their options: where your workspaces folder is and the build settings. The file is optional; without it, the commands use the folder workspaces and the defaults.

This page is a reference. It lists where the commands look for the file, every key, how values are read, example files and the error messages. The options of each command are in the Command reference.

docs.title: Words used on this page
docs.text: Word Meaning workspaces folder The folder of Python files that create your workspaces. The workspaces: key names it, or lists the files and folders to build instead. built workspace The folder that buildzr build writes for one workspace: the viewer, the model data and a file called build.json. build output The folder that holds every built workspace. The build.out key names it. data-only workspace A built workspace without the viewer, only the model data.

docs.title: How the commands use this file
docs.text:
Each setting comes from the first of these that has it:

  1. An option on the command line.
  2. buildzr.yaml.
  3. The built-in default.

When workspaces: is a list, an entry can set its own build settings, which come between the option and the build: section; see Choosing which files to build.

No environment variable sets a setting directly. You can use environment variables only inside the file, as ${VAR}.

buildzr build and buildzr serve read the whole file, so a problem anywhere in it stops either command. build uses workspaces and build; it never uses serve. When you give serve a folder that already holds built workspaces, it uses only the serve settings of the file.

When the file has a problem, the command prints every problem, one per line, and exits with code 2. Examples of error messages shows the format.

docs.title: Where the commands find the file
docs.text:
Without the -c option, a command looks for the file as follows:

  • It starts in the current folder and walks up to the parent folders. The first buildzr.yaml it finds is used.
  • It stops after the folder that contains .git, so it never reads a file outside your Git repository.
  • The name must be exactly buildzr.yaml. If a folder has buildzr.yml or .buildzr.yaml and no buildzr.yaml, the search stops with found buildzr.yml; the config file must be named buildzr.yaml.

Relative paths in the file are relative to the folder that holds the file, not to the current folder. Without a file, the default folders workspaces and .buildzr/build are relative to the current folder.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Type Default Meaning version integer 1 The version of the file format. Only 1 is accepted. workspaces text (path), or a list workspaces The workspaces folder. A path to a single .py file also works. Or a list of files and folders to build, each with its own build settings: see Choosing which files to build. -w on the command line replaces it. workspaces[].path text (path) none In a list: a .py file, or a folder whose Python files are all built. An entry that is only a path is the same as an entry with only path. workspaces[].build k, text_color, viewer none In a list: the build settings of this entry’s workspaces. Each one wins over the same key of build. out is not allowed here. build.k whole number, at least 1 4 Room for a box that contains other boxes, as a multiple of the area of an empty box; the same value as --k. See Choosing a value for --k. build.text_color wcag or c4 wcag The text colour on boxes. See --text-color in buildzr build. build.viewer true / false true false builds data-only workspaces. build.out text (path) .buildzr/build The build output: build writes one folder per workspace into it, and serve serves it. serve.public_url text (http:// or https:// URL) none The address at which readers reach the server, for example behind a proxy; the same value as --public-url. The links of the Model API (viewerUrl, apiUrl) start with it. A / at the end is dropped. Without it, the links start with /. serve.port whole number, 1 to 65535 8000 The port serve listens on; the same value as -p/--port. serve.host text 127.0.0.1 The address serve listens on; the same value as --host. 127.0.0.1 lets only this machine connect. 0.0.0.0 shares the server with every machine on the network, and serve has no login, so set it only on purpose. serve.cors_origins list of text [] The web origins (https://host[:port], no path, no *) whose pages may read the Model API from a browser; the same values as repeated --cors-origin. An empty list means none. --cors-origin on the command line replaces this list; it does not add to it.

Unknown keys are errors. Secrets never go in this file: the keys token, password and secret are refused.

Keys of older versions are refused with a line that says what to do: workspace (use workspaces), and targets and default_target (buildzr deploy no longer exists).

To let your editor check the file, use the JSON Schema buildzr/site/schema/config.schema.json. Add # yaml-language-server: $schema=<path or URL of the schema> as the first line of the file.

docs.title: Values from environment variables
docs.text:
You can use environment variables in the text values workspaces (also each path of a list), build.out, serve.public_url, serve.host and each entry of serve.cors_origins. Not in serve.port, which is a number.

  • Write ${NAME}, where NAME matches [A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*. Write ${NAME:-fallback} to use fallback when the variable is unset or empty. Write $$ for a literal $. Any other $ is an error.
  • A variable that is unset or empty, and has no fallback, is an error.
  • A value is expanded only when a command uses it.

docs.title: How the file is read
docs.text:
The file is YAML, read with stricter rules than most YAML tools use:

  • Only true, false, null, plain decimal integers (4) and plain decimal numbers (1.5) are typed. Everything else is text, including yes, no, on, off, y, n, 0755, 1:30 and dates. A key on: stays the text on.
  • Types are checked, not converted: k: "4" is an error.
  • Duplicate keys, anchors (&a), aliases (*a), << merges and !tags are errors.
  • All problems are listed at once, each as buildzr.yaml:<line>: <key>: <message>.

docs.title: Example files
docs.text:
A project whose models live in another folder:

workspaces: architecture

A project that builds data-only workspaces, with more room for boxes that contain other boxes, into a folder named after the Git branch:

version: 1
workspaces: architecture
build:
  k: 9
  viewer: false
  out: "public/${BRANCH:-main}"

Settings for buildzr serve on a shared machine behind a proxy. Each one is used only when its option is not given on the command line. Set public_url in the file when the same project is served at a different address in each environment, such as a preview per branch: the variable gives the address, so the command stays the same everywhere.

serve:
  public_url: "https://${PREVIEW_HOST:-architecture.example.com}"
  port: 8080
  host: 0.0.0.0
  cors_origins:
    - https://dashboard.example.com

docs.title: A project with several workspace files
docs.text:
A project can keep many model files in its workspaces folder, and one file can create several workspaces. This project has three workspaces in two files. Serve your workspaces builds and serves the same project step by step.

my-project/
├── buildzr.yaml
└── architecture/
    ├── billing.py      creates the workspace Billing
    └── platform.py     creates the workspaces Core and Infra

buildzr.yaml names the workspaces folder:

workspaces: architecture

architecture/billing.py creates one workspace:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace("Billing") as w:
    invoicing = SoftwareSystem("Invoicing")
    payments = SoftwareSystem("Payment Provider")
    invoicing >> "Collects payments through" >> payments

architecture/platform.py creates two:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace("Core") as core:
    customer = Person("Customer")
    shop = SoftwareSystem("Web Shop")
    payments = SoftwareSystem("Payment Provider")
    customer >> "Buys from" >> shop
    shop >> "Takes payments through" >> payments

with Workspace("Infra") as infra:
    cluster = SoftwareSystem("Kubernetes Cluster")
    database = SoftwareSystem("Database Service")
    cluster >> "Stores data in" >> database

Build the project. Every workspace of every file gets its own built workspace:

$ buildzr build
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)
built .buildzr/build/core (3 elements, 2 relationships, 0 views; modelHash sha256:baa7b6d1e769…)
built .buildzr/build/infra (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:16a0df17df2a…)

The build output then holds one folder per workspace:

.buildzr/build/
├── billing/    build.json, index.html, assets/, data/
├── core/       build.json, index.html, assets/, data/
└── infra/      build.json, index.html, assets/, data/

buildzr serve finds all three up to date and serves each one at its own address:

$ buildzr serve
up to date: billing, core, infra
Serving .buildzr/build at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/billing/
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/core/
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/infra/
Workspace list at http://127.0.0.1:8000/_buildzr/v1/workspaces

What to know about such a project:

  • Folder names come from workspace names, not from file names: Workspace("Core") in platform.py becomes core, at /core/. The naming rule lowers the case and replaces spaces and other characters with -.

  • Two workspaces with the same name stop the build before anything is written. If architecture/legacy.py also created Workspace("billing"), build would print, with the full path of your workspaces folder:

    buildzr: error: two workspaces would both be built as "billing": "Billing" in billing.py and "billing" in legacy.py (paths in /home/me/my-project/architecture); rename one of them

    The same error appears when one model file imports another, for example from billing import invoicing in legacy.py: the import runs the with Workspace("Billing") block of billing.py again, so legacy.py creates a second Billing workspace.

  • -w with one file builds only that file and removes nothing, not even the built workspaces of files you deleted:

    $ buildzr build -w architecture/billing.py
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)

  • A broken file breaks only its own workspaces. With a typo in the last line of platform.py, Core and Infra are broken and Billing is built as usual. The build exits with code 1:

    from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace("Core") as core:
    customer = Person("Customer")
    shop = SoftwareSystem("Web Shop")
    payments = SoftwareSystem("Payment Provider")
    customer >> "Buys from" >> shop
    shop >> "Takes payments through" >> payments

with Workspace("Infra") as infra:
    cluster = SoftwareSystem("Kubernetes Cluster")
    database = SoftwareSystem("Database Service")
    cluster >> "Stores data in" >> databse


    $ buildzr build
...
NameError: name 'databse' is not defined
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)
buildzr: BROKEN: workspace core (architecture/platform.py) failed at the model step
    NameError: name 'databse' is not defined
    platform.py, line 13: cluster >> "Stores data in" >> databse
  this workspace is broken; the viewer says so
buildzr: BROKEN: workspace infra (architecture/platform.py) failed at the model step
    NameError: name 'databse' is not defined
    platform.py, line 13: cluster >> "Stores data in" >> databse
  this workspace is broken; the viewer says so
[exit code 1]

    Core is broken too, although the error is in the part that creates Infra: when a file fails, none of its workspaces can be trusted. serve lists the broken workspaces next to the good one, and the list for programs gives each one its status:

    GET /_buildzr/v1/workspaces


    {
  "apiVersion": "1",
  "workspaces": [
    {
      "name": "billing",
      "path": "/billing/",
      "workspaceName": "Billing",
      "status": "ok",
      "viewerUrl": "/billing/",
      "apiUrl": "/billing/api/v1/",
      "llmsUrl": "/billing/llms.txt",
      "modelHash": "sha256:4b0dfb4153c1e2f16f2d94c116fc6c70c705b5935e51069616ec8f3e30feac0b",
      "builtAt": "2026-10-18T16:45:54Z",
      "source": "billing.py"
    },
    {
      "name": "core",
      "path": "/core/",
      "workspaceName": "Core",
      "status": "broken",
      "viewerUrl": "/core/",
      "apiUrl": "/core/api/v1/",
      "llmsUrl": "/core/llms.txt",
      "modelHash": null,
      "builtAt": "2026-10-18T16:45:54Z",
      "source": "platform.py",
      "stage": "model",
      "errors": [
        "NameError: name 'databse' is not defined",
        "platform.py, line 13: cluster >> \"Stores data in\" >> databse"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "infra",
      "path": "/infra/",
      "workspaceName": "Infra",
      "status": "broken",
      "viewerUrl": "/infra/",
      "apiUrl": "/infra/api/v1/",
      "llmsUrl": "/infra/llms.txt",
      "modelHash": null,
      "builtAt": "2026-10-18T16:45:54Z",
      "source": "platform.py",
      "stage": "model",
      "errors": [
        "NameError: name 'databse' is not defined",
        "platform.py, line 13: cluster >> \"Stores data in\" >> databse"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

    Fix the typo and build again: all three are ok. When a workspace is broken has the details.

    from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace("Core") as core:
    customer = Person("Customer")
    shop = SoftwareSystem("Web Shop")
    payments = SoftwareSystem("Payment Provider")
    customer >> "Buys from" >> shop
    shop >> "Takes payments through" >> payments

with Workspace("Infra") as infra:
    cluster = SoftwareSystem("Kubernetes Cluster")
    database = SoftwareSystem("Database Service")
    cluster >> "Stores data in" >> database


    $ buildzr build
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)
built .buildzr/build/core (3 elements, 2 relationships, 0 views; modelHash sha256:baa7b6d1e769…)
built .buildzr/build/infra (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:16a0df17df2a…)

docs.title: Choosing which files to build
docs.text:
With workspaces: architecture, every model file of the folder is built, and every workspace gets the same build settings. To build only some files, or to give one file its own settings, make workspaces: a list of files and folders.

This continues the project above. The team adds architecture/api_catalog.py, a list of the services and their APIs that scripts and AI assistants read through the Model API. Nobody looks at it in a browser, so it needs no viewer:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace("API Catalog") as w:
    orders = SoftwareSystem("Orders API", "REST, owned by the shop team")
    invoices = SoftwareSystem("Invoices API", "REST, owned by the billing team")
    payments = SoftwareSystem("Payment Provider", "External")
    orders >> "Asks for an invoice through" >> invoices
    invoices >> "Collects payments through" >> payments

my-project/
├── buildzr.yaml
└── architecture/
    ├── api_catalog.py  creates the workspace API Catalog
    ├── billing.py      creates the workspace Billing
    └── platform.py     creates the workspaces Core and Infra

This buildzr.yaml lists the three model files. Platform diagrams have systems inside other systems, so platform.py gets more room for them (k: 9); the catalog is built without the viewer:

build:
  k: 4
workspaces:
  - architecture/billing.py
  - path: architecture/platform.py
    build:
      k: 9
  - path: architecture/api_catalog.py
    build:
      viewer: false

Each entry is a path, or a mapping with path and an optional build that holds k, text_color or viewer. The built line of a workspace shows the settings that are not the defaults:

$ buildzr build
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)
built .buildzr/build/core (k 9; 3 elements, 2 relationships, 0 views; modelHash sha256:baa7b6d1e769…)
built .buildzr/build/infra (k 9; 2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:16a0df17df2a…)
built .buildzr/build/api-catalog (data only; 3 elements, 2 relationships, 0 views; modelHash sha256:ae661bde471c…)

serve serves the data-only workspace like the others, but gives the address of its Model API instead of a viewer:

$ buildzr serve
up to date: api-catalog, billing, core, infra
Serving .buildzr/build at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/api-catalog/api/v1/ (data only, no viewer)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/billing/
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/core/
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/infra/
Workspace list at http://127.0.0.1:8000/_buildzr/v1/workspaces

The index page at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ links the Model API of the catalog, and in the workspace list for programs its viewerUrl is null.

The index page with the data-only workspace api-catalog: it has no viewer link.

How a list works:

  • Only the listed files are built. A model file in architecture that is not on the list is not built. Paths are relative to the folder that holds buildzr.yaml, and they may use environment variables.

  • A folder entry builds every model file in it, as a workspaces folder does: its subfolders too, and not the files and folders whose name starts with _ or .. Its build settings apply to each of those files:

    workspaces:
  - architecture/billing.py
  - path: shared-models/
    build:
      text_color: c4

    A folder entry that holds no model file prints a warning and builds nothing; the other entries are built as usual.

  • Each setting of a workspace comes from the first of these that has it:

    1. An option on the command line: --k, --text-color, --no-viewer.
    2. The build of the file’s entry.
    3. The build section of the file.
    4. The built-in default.
  • -w replaces the list. buildzr build -w architecture/platform.py builds that file with the settings of the build section, so with k 4, not 9. To build one file with the settings of its entry, run buildzr build without -w.
  • A change to one entry rebuilds only its workspaces. The settings of each workspace are part of its fingerprint. Change k: 9 to k: 12, and serve builds Core and Infra again and finds Billing and API Catalog up to date.

  • Taking a file off the list removes its built workspace on the next full build, as deleting the file does with a workspaces folder. Without the api_catalog.py entry:

    build:
  k: 4
workspaces:
  - architecture/billing.py
  - path: architecture/platform.py
    build:
      k: 9

    $ buildzr build
built .buildzr/build/billing (2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:4b0dfb4153c1…)
built .buildzr/build/core (k 9; 3 elements, 2 relationships, 0 views; modelHash sha256:baa7b6d1e769…)
built .buildzr/build/infra (k 9; 2 elements, 1 relationship, 0 views; modelHash sha256:16a0df17df2a…)
removed api-catalog: its model file architecture/api_catalog.py is no longer in the workspaces: list

    buildzr build -w FILE and serve never remove anything. A build removes only the workspaces it built itself: build.json records the config file of the list, so a build of another config file, or of a single path with -w, never removes the workspaces of this list.

  • A path that does not exist stops the command before anything is built, with the line of the entry. With a typo in the first entry:

    workspaces:
  - architecture/biling.py
  - architecture/platform.py

    $ buildzr build
buildzr.yaml:2: workspaces[0]: architecture/biling.py not found (relative to buildzr.yaml's folder)
[exit code 2]

    Entries are counted from 0: workspaces[0] is the first one.

  • A file may be on the list only once, also through a folder entry. Both entries are named:

    workspaces:
  - architecture/platform.py
  - path: architecture
    build:
      k: 9

    $ buildzr build
buildzr.yaml:3: workspaces[1]: architecture holds architecture/platform.py, which is already in workspaces[0] (line 2); list each file once
[exit code 2]

    An empty list (workspaces: []) is an error too.

docs.title: Examples of error messages
docs.text:
Each message names the line of the file and the key it is about.

A value of the wrong type:

workspaces: architecture
build:
  k: four

buildzr.yaml:3: build.k: expected a whole number of at least 1, got the text "four"

A secret in the file. The message tells you where to keep it instead:

workspaces: architecture
build:
  token: abc123

buildzr.yaml:3: build: unknown key "token". Secrets never go in this file; keep them in an environment variable.

A file written for an older version:

workspace: architecture/model.py
targets:
  www: {dir: /var/www/architecture}

buildzr.yaml:1: workspace: removed: use workspaces: (a folder; a single .py file path also works)
buildzr.yaml:2: targets: removed: buildzr deploy no longer exists; delete this key

An environment variable that is not set. This uses the second example file above, with out: "public/${BRANCH}" and no fallback:

workspaces: architecture
build:
  out: "public/${BRANCH}"

$ buildzr build
buildzr.yaml:3: build.out: environment variable BRANCH is not set (used in "public/${BRANCH}")
[exit code 2]

The last line of each command example, such as [exit code 2], shows the exit code. The command does not print it.

docs.title: Python functions
docs.text: The module buildzr.site.config has these functions for scripts and tests: find_config(start), load_config(path), resolve_workspaces(cfg, env), resolve_workspace_entries(cfg, env) (a list of workspaces:, or None), workspace_files(cfg, entries) (the model files of each entry; it checks that they exist and are listed once), resolve_build(cfg, env) and resolve_serve(cfg, env). Problems raise ConfigError. load_config does not read environment variables; the resolve_* functions do.

docs.title: Contributing to buildzr
docs.text:
Thank you for considering contributing to buildzr! Your help is greatly appreciated. Below are some guidelines to help you get started.

Happy Hacking 👩‍💻!

docs.title: Codespaces
docs.text:
I recommend using GitHub Codespaces for development. Codespaces provides a consistent development environment and simplifies the setup process.

You can quickly set up and start contributing to our project using GitHub Codespaces via GitHub CLI. Follow these steps:

  1. Install the GitHub CLI if you haven’t already. Visit https://cli.github.com/.

  2. Authenticate with your GitHub account by running:

    gh auth login

  3. Create a new codespace for this repository using the following command:

    gh codespace create -r amirulmenjeni/buildzr

  4. Once the codespace is created, you can connect to it via VS Code or ssh into it:

    gh codespace ssh

  5. Inside the workspace, sync the locked Python environment:

    uv sync --all-extras --locked

    Run project commands through the environment with uv run, for example:

    uv run pytest --mypy tests

The codespace environment also includes useful tools developed by the Structurizr team such as Structurizr CLI, Structurizr Lite, and Structurizr On-Premises to view diagrams defined in Structurizr DSL or in Structurizr JSON. They’re mostly helpful during development to validate the Structurizr JSON generated by buildzr (see Structurizr).

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
All tests are located in the tests folder. To run the tests, use the following command: 

uv run pytest --mypy tests

python -m buildzr.site.check DATA_DIR checks the data/ folder of one built workspace (for example .buildzr/build/shop/data) against the data contract: the JSON schemas in buildzr/site/schema/ plus what they cannot express, such as canonical bytes, containment, counts, frames and ports. It prints OK or each error and exits 1 on errors. buildzr build runs the same check on every workspace it builds and writes a broken workspace when it fails, so the command is for contributors who want to check a data folder on its own. jsonschema, which it needs, is a normal dependency of buildzr.

docs.title: Testing buildzr Samples
docs.text:
Sometimes it is valuable to manually check the output of the Structurizr workspace generated by buildzr visually. For this reason, you can create buildzr samples in the tests/samples directory.

Here’s an example of a simple workspace to showcase the group feature in Structurizr DSL used for grouping elements together:

from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Container,
    Component,
    Group,
    SystemLandscapeView,
    SystemContextView,
    ContainerView,
)

with Workspace("w") as w:
    with Group("Company 1"):
        system_a = SoftwareSystem("A")
        with system_a:
            a1 = Container("a1")
            a2 = Container("a2")

    with Group("Company 2"):
        system_b = SoftwareSystem("B")
        with system_b:
            b1 = Container("b1")
            b2 = Container("b2")
            with b2:
                c1 = Component("c1")

    system_c = SoftwareSystem("C")

    # Define relationships
    system_a >> "Uses" >> system_b
    a1 >> "Uses" >> b1
    system_a >> "Uses" >> system_c

    # Create views
    SystemLandscapeView(
        key='groups-sample',
        description="Groups Sample"
    )

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=system_a,
        key='groups-sample-a',
        description="Groups Sample - Software System A"
    )

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=system_b,
        key='groups-sample-b',
        description="Groups Sample - Software System B"
    )

    ContainerView(
        software_system_selector=system_b,
        key='groups-sample-b2',
        description="Groups Sample - Container B2"
    )

    # Export to JSON
    w.to_json('groups-sample.json')

The example above demonstrates the current buildzr API using context managers (with statements) for a cleaner, more Pythonic syntax. Key features shown:

  • Use with Workspace("name") as w: to create a workspace context
  • Use with Group("name"): to group elements together
  • Use with software_system: or with container: to nest containers and components
  • Define relationships using the >> operator
  • Views and styles are created within the workspace context
  • Export using w.to_json('filename.json')

You can run this code directly or create sample files in the tests/samples directory for testing purposes.

docs.title: Working with the .json files
docs.text:
What can you do with the generated .json files?

As mentioned, the .json file, if successfully and correctly generated using buildzr, should follow the Structurizr JSON schema. Thus you can make use of existing and mature Structurizr tools such as the Structurizr CLI and Structurizr Lite.

If you use codespaces (highly recommended), these tools are already pre-installed in the devcontainer image.

For example, to export the tests/samples/.tests.samples.groups.json to other format (say, PlantUML):

structurizr.sh \
    export \
    --format plantuml \
    --workspace tests/samples/.tests.samples.groups.json \
    --output tests/samples/.tests.samples.groups.puml

To view the rendering of tests/samples/.tests.samples.groups.json in the browser at http://localhost:8080:

structurizr-lite.sh tests/samples/.tests.samples.groups.json

docs.title: Using Structurizr On-Premises
docs.text:
Structurizr On-Premises provides a full-featured workspace server with API support, allowing you to publish and manage multiple workspaces. This is useful for testing workspace publishing, API integration, and multi-workspace scenarios.

The codespace includes a helper script to run Structurizr On-Premises via Docker:

# Start Structurizr On-Premises (available at http://localhost:8080)
structurizr-onpremises.sh start

# Check status
structurizr-onpremises.sh status

# View logs
structurizr-onpremises.sh logs

# Stop the server
structurizr-onpremises.sh stop

Default credentials: structurizr / password

Once running, you can publish workspaces using the Structurizr CLI:

# Publish a workspace
structurizr.sh push \
    -id 1 \
    -key YOUR_API_KEY \
    -secret YOUR_API_SECRET \
    -workspace workspace.json \
    -url http://localhost:8080/api

Data is persisted in ~/.structurizr-onpremises/ so your workspaces survive container restarts.

docs.title: Working on the documentation
docs.text: The documentation is a MkDocs site. Its pages are the Markdown files under docs/, and mkdocs.yml configures it. The docs workflow builds the site with --strict and deploys it to GitHub Pages on every push to master. The public address is https://buildzr.dev.

docs.title: Set up the environment
docs.text:
Work in the devcontainer of the repository; it has the same Python, uv and Java tools as CI. Install every extra, which includes the docs extra:

uv sync --all-extras --locked

uv sync --extra docs also installs the documentation tools, but it removes the other extras from the environment, and the tests that need them, such as the PlantUML export tests, fail. uv sync --all-extras --locked brings them back.

The documentation tests build the examples of the pages with the real layout when Node.js 18 or newer is on PATH and the viewer is built ((cd viewer && npm ci && npm run build)). Without them, the tests lay the examples out with a stand-in that draws nothing real; the commands, their output and the Model API answers are still checked.

The documentation build also needs the files of the Run Code button (see Python examples and Run Code). Build them once, and again after you change the viewer or the Python of buildzr; this needs Node.js 22:

(cd viewer && npm ci)
uv run python scripts/build_docs_assets.py

The script builds the viewer and writes everything into docs/runcode/, which Git ignores. Without that folder, mkdocs build and mkdocs serve stop with a message that names this command.

docs.title: Preview and check your changes
docs.text:
uv run mkdocs serve serves the site at http://127.0.0.1:8000 and reloads it when you save a file.

Before you submit, run the strict build and the documentation tests. The strict build fails on any warning, such as a broken link. The documentation tests check the links between pages and run the examples in the pages.

uv run mkdocs build --strict
uv run pytest tests/docs

docs.title: Edit the roadmap
docs.text: The roadmap is the data file roadmap.yml in the repository root; there is no Markdown to edit. The docs build (scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py) validates the file and renders it into the page, and stops with a list of every fault if the file breaks the schema. Move an item between active, planned and launched instead of copying it, and base a launched entry on a release tag or merged pull request. The Structurizr feature tables are a separate page, docs/structurizr-compatibility.md.

docs.title: Add a page
docs.text: Create a Markdown file under docs/ and add it to the nav section of mkdocs.yml. A page that is not in nav does not appear in the menu.

docs.title: Python examples and Run Code
docs.text:
Every python code block of the documentation gets a Run Code button. When a reader presses it, the browser downloads Python (Pyodide, about 6 MB from cdn.jsdelivr.net, once) and a small build of buildzr, runs the example, and draws its workspace in the buildzr viewer under the code. The diagram is built with the same steps as buildzr build, so it looks the same as in buildzr serve. Nothing is downloaded until the first press.

Write each example so that it runs on its own:

  • An example may be a fragment. Run Code adds from buildzr.dsl import * when the example imports nothing from buildzr.dsl, and puts an example without with Workspace(...) as w: inside one.
  • The diagram shows the last Workspace the example creates.
  • An error shows the line number as the page shows it, with the message.

Two comments control the button:

Comment Where Effect # no-run: <reason> First line of the block No Run Code button. Use it for code that cannot run in a browser, such as an export to PlantUML or code that reads a file, and give the reason (tests/docs/test_snippets.py checks it). The line is hidden. # focus: <element id> Any line The viewer opens on this element, selected. The id is the viewer’s id, such as shop/database. The line is hidden and not copied. # focus: view:<key> Any line The viewer opens on the view with this key.

Without # focus:, the viewer opens on a deployment or dynamic view that the example defines; otherwise on the landscape, with the last element created that has children expanded; otherwise on the whole landscape. Add # focus: only when a page is about one element that this rule does not pick.

To check the examples of a page in a real browser, use run_page_blocks of tests/docs/browser.py in a test; tests/docs/test_runcode_browser.py shows how. These tests need Node.js, the Chromium of the viewer tests ((cd viewer && npx playwright install chromium)), the built Run Code files and a connection to cdn.jsdelivr.net; without them they are skipped.

docs.title: Submitting Changes
docs.text: As usual, just fork the repo, make changes, and submit PRs!

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: The release workflow publishes releases from master. It never pushes commits to master.

docs.title: Cut a release
docs.text: Open a pull request that sets a final version, for example 1.0.1, in buildzr/__about__.py. When the pull request is merged, the workflow builds the viewer and the package, checks them, publishes the package to PyPI and pushes the tag v1.0.1.

docs.title: Cut a release candidate
docs.text:
Do the same with a version such as 1.1.0rc1. Versions follow PEP 440, and rc is the only pre-release kind that is released. Number the candidates rc1, rc2, and so on; the final 1.1.0 sorts after them. The tag of 1.1.0rc1 is v1.1.0rc1.

PyPI does not offer a release candidate to a plain pip install buildzr. Install it with one of these commands:

  • uvx --from buildzr==1.1.0rc1 buildzr build
  • uv add buildzr==1.1.0rc1
  • pip install buildzr==1.1.0rc1
  • pip install --pre buildzr

docs.title: Which pushes release
docs.text: Every push to master runs the workflow. It releases only when the version is final or a release candidate, and its tag does not exist yet. The workflow skips development, alpha, beta and post-release versions, such as 1.0.1.dev0, 1.0.1a1, 1.0.1b1 or 1.0.1.post1. Bumping the version to .dev0 therefore does not trigger a release.

docs.title: What the workflow checks before it publishes
docs.text:
The viewer (viewer/) is built into the gitignored folder buildzr/site/static/ and ships inside the package. The workflow therefore runs npm ci and npm run build in viewer/ before uv build.

Then .github/scripts/check_wheel.py dist --sdist fails the run, before anything is published, unless both the sdist and the wheel contain the viewer, its copy of the third-party notices, the JSON schemas, the modules of buildzr build and buildzr serve and the layout’s Node runner with elkjs, and the version of the wheel equals buildzr/__about__.py. It also requires THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt in the .dist-info/licenses/ folder of the wheel and at the root of the sdist (license-files in pyproject.toml puts it there). To check a build yourself:

(cd viewer && npm ci && npm run build)
uv build
python .github/scripts/check_wheel.py dist --sdist

docs.title: Third-party notices
docs.text:
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt holds the licence text and copyright notice of everything from others that the package ships: the npm packages linked into the viewer bundle, the Inter font and the vendored elkjs. The viewer’s About dialog shows the same file. It is generated; do not edit it. After you change the production dependencies of viewer/package.json, the Inter files or the elkjs bundle, run this from the repository root, then commit the result:

(cd viewer && npm ci)
python scripts/gen_third_party_notices.py

tests/site/test_notices.py fails when a package of the bundle is missing from the file or the file is out of date. Dependencies that are only type declarations (@types/*, csstype) or build tools are not listed, because their code is not shipped. The Java libraries of the PlantUML export are not shipped either; they are downloaded on first use.

docs.title: The smoke test of the wheel
docs.text:
Pull requests that change the package also run a smoke test in the build workflow. It installs the built wheel into a new virtual environment and, in a temporary project with two model files in workspaces/, runs buildzr build and buildzr serve, then fetches the list page, both workspaces, a Model API answer and the list of workspaces. A second project with one workspace checks that / redirects to it, and a last step builds with uvx --from the wheel. To run it locally, run the three commands above first. The smoke test needs uv, Node.js 18 or newer and curl.

.github/scripts/smoke_wheel.sh dist

docs.title: The version check on pull requests
docs.text:
When a pull request changes the version, the check_version job of the build workflow checks the version before the merge. It fails on:

  • a version that is not canonical PEP 440, for example 0.0.033;
  • a final version or release candidate that already has a tag;
  • a version that is not higher than the latest v* tag. For example, 1.1.0rc2 is higher than 1.1.0rc1, and 1.1.0 is higher than 1.1.0rc2, but 1.1.0rc3 is not higher than the released 1.1.0.

Otherwise, the job reports whether the merge will release the version to PyPI.

docs.title: If a release fails
docs.text:
If a release fails, no tag is pushed. Re-run the failed run from the Actions tab before you merge anything else. Otherwise, the next push to master releases that version from the newer commit.

A re-run skips files that are already on PyPI, so a re-run after a failed tag push only pushes the tag. A version that reached PyPI cannot be uploaded again: fix forward with a new version.

docs.title: Try buildzr in your browser
docs.text:
Edit the Python model and press Run.

The demo needs JavaScript. Without it, try buildzr with a local install.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Your code runs in this browser tab. Nothing you type is sent to a server. It runs with the permissions of this page, so run code you wrote or read, never code a stranger asked you to paste. The demo never runs code on its own.
  • A run ends after 30 seconds. Press Stop (or Esc) to end it sooner. Press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) to run.
  • You get the viewer and the model JSON, not Java-based exports. PlantUML, SVG and PNG export need Java, so use Copy model JSON here and export locally for the rest.
  • Python has only the standard library and buildzr. If your code creates several workspaces, the last one is drawn.
How it works
  • Python runs in a Web Worker through Pyodide, so the page stays responsive. buildzr builds the workspace as buildzr build does, and the viewer is the one buildzr serve shows. Without a Web Worker the demo does not run, because it could not stop a runaway loop.
  • The first run downloads about 6 MB (Python from cdn.jsdelivr.net, the viewer from this site). Your browser keeps them, so later runs are fast. Offline, you can keep editing, but you need one online run first.
  • Your code is kept in this browser’s local storage, so a reload does not lose it. Reset returns to the example you loaded last.
  • When you run again, the viewer keeps your place. A line such as # focus: shop/api or # focus: view:production picks where it opens the first time; see Viewer links.
  • Code is limited to 50,000 characters and printed output to 20,000. The editor is plain text, so type spaces to indent and press Tab to move on.

docs.title: Hosting the built workspaces elsewhere
docs.text: buildzr serve is the simplest way to let people open your workspaces, but you may already have a web server, or a static host that publishes a folder. This page says which parts of a built workspace work there and which need buildzr serve, and how to copy the build output.

docs.title: Words used on this page
docs.text: Word Meaning built workspace The folder that buildzr build writes for one workspace: the viewer, the model data and build.json. build output The folder that holds every built workspace, one subfolder per workspace. Default: .buildzr/build. static host Any web server that only sends files as they are, such as nginx, Apache, GitHub Pages or an object store with web hosting.

docs.title: What works without buildzr serve
docs.text:
A built workspace uses relative addresses only, so it works at any path of any web server:

Part On a static host Why The viewer (index.html, assets/) Works The viewer loads its scripts with relative addresses (./assets/...). The model data (data/index.json, data/model.<hash>.json, data/scene/...) Works The viewer reads only these files, with relative addresses. Viewer links (#/m/..., #/v/...) Work The part after # never reaches the server. See Viewer links. The Model API (api/v1/) Does not work buildzr serve computes each answer; there are no files for it. llms.txt Does not work buildzr serve generates it from the model. The list of workspaces at / and /_buildzr/v1/workspaces Does not work buildzr serve makes them from the build output. Link to each workspace yourself. The Workspace selector of the viewer Not shown The viewer fills it from /_buildzr/v1/workspaces, and only when buildzr serve said in a response header that the list exists. A static host sends no such header, so the viewer asks for nothing and shows no selector. Link to each workspace yourself.

A static host that shows the files of a folder at its address also shows build.json, which holds the version of buildzr, the build options, whether the workspace is broken (with its errors), the path of the model file inside your workspaces folder and the path of the workspaces folder relative to the build output. Nothing else of your project is in a built workspace.

A broken workspace works on a static host too: its viewer reads build.json and shows that it is broken. See When a workspace is broken.

docs.title: Copy the build output
docs.text:
Build first, then copy the content of the build output to the folder that your web server publishes. With rsync, --delete also removes workspaces that you no longer build:

buildzr build
rsync -a --delete .buildzr/build/ host:/var/www/architecture/

Each workspace is then at https://<your host>/architecture/<name>/. Link to it with the trailing /: the viewer loads its files relative to that address, so /architecture/<name> without the / works only where the web server adds it.

buildzr build writes each workspace to a temporary folder first and renames it into place, so the build output itself is never half written. A copy is not atomic: while rsync runs, a reader may get files of the old and the new build for a moment. Reloading the page fixes it.

docs.title: When you need the Model API
docs.text:
If scripts or AI assistants must ask questions about the model, run buildzr serve with the build output, on the server or behind your web server:

buildzr serve --no-build --host 127.0.0.1 --public-url https://architecture.example.com

--no-build serves the folder as it is, so the server needs neither the model files nor Node. Point your web server’s proxy at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. Serve your workspaces explains --public-url and --cors-origin.

docs.title: Model API
docs.text:
The Model API answers questions about your architecture as JSON. Scripts, CI (continuous integration) jobs, dashboards, AI assistants, or a person with curl, can ask “what talks to the database?” without opening the viewer and without reading the Python code of the model.

buildzr serve provides a Model API for every workspace it serves, at api/v1/ below the address of the workspace: the workspace microservices-example has its viewer at /microservices-example/ and its Model API at /microservices-example/api/v1/. The API is read-only: it answers only GET and HEAD requests.

This page is a reference of the API: the orientation document, every endpoint with an example, the limits, the errors, caching, browser access and the links to the viewer.

docs.title: Start buildzr serve with the Model API
docs.text:
Serve a workspace; buildzr serve builds it first. Here, the model file is examples/buildzr_models_example.py from the buildzr repository:

$ buildzr serve examples/buildzr_models_example.py
built .buildzr/build/microservices-example (25 elements, 8 relationships, 2 views; modelHash sha256:1e2b294431af…)
Serving .buildzr/build at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/microservices-example/
Workspace list at http://127.0.0.1:8000/_buildzr/v1/workspaces

Then send a request with any HTTP client, for example curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/microservices-example/api/v1/. The answer is the orientation document.

The examples on this page are real answers from that workspace. They show the default output of buildzr serve, without --public-url. In the text, paths such as api/v1/tree are relative to the address of the workspace.

docs.title: Words used on this page
docs.text: Word Meaning element A person, a software system, a container (an application or data store inside a system) or a component (a part inside a container). Custom elements (type Element, such as a device) and deployment elements are elements too (see the next rows). custom element An element outside the C4 hierarchy, such as a piece of hardware. Its type is Element; it has no parent and no children. When the model gives it metadata (the word in brackets under its name in a diagram), the element answer has a metadata field; without metadata there is no such field. deployment element A deployment node (a server, cluster, region…), an infrastructure node (a load balancer, DNS…), or a container or software system instance (that container or system running on a node). Its id starts with deploy/<environment>/, for example deploy/production/aws/ecs-cluster/web-app. id The element’s path of lower-case names, joined by /: e-commerce-system/web-app is the Web App inside the E-Commerce System. Two siblings with the same name get -2, -3. Ids are given in query parameters: ?id=e-commerce-system/web-app. relationship An explicit “A uses B” statement written in the model, with a description and sometimes a technology. Its id is <source id>-><destination id>, plus :<description> when two relationships connect the same pair. rollup An arrow between two big boxes stands for every relationship between what is inside them. This API follows the same rule as the viewer: a relationship of a descendant counts for its ancestors. view A diagram the authors chose to draw (for example a system context view), as opposed to the free browsing the viewer offers. modelHash A fingerprint of the model, shown as sha256: and a hash. The same model always has the same hash, and every answer carries it. workspace A Workspace(...) written in Python. buildzr serve serves each one at /<name>/, with its own Model API. viewer The web page of a workspace that draws the diagrams. A data-only workspace has no viewer.

docs.title: The orientation document
docs.text:
GET api/v1/ returns the orientation document. It tells a reader what the model is, how big it is, and which requests it can send. Start here.

GET /microservices-example/api/v1/

{
  "apiVersion": "1",
  "modelHash": "sha256:1e2b294431af70f6e5e43dbc369f543289ebdcc373d65f9b4fdeb4fcb3c53df6",
  "name": "microservices-example",
  "description": null,
  "status": "ok",
  "builtWith": {
    "buildzr": "1.1.1",
    "k": 4
  },
  "counts": {
    "elements": 25,
    "relationships": 8,
    "views": 2,
    "byType": {
      "Component": 4,
      "Container": 5,
      "ContainerInstance": 5,
      "DeploymentNode": 6,
      "InfrastructureNode": 1,
      "Person": 2,
      "SoftwareSystem": 2
    }
  },
  "tags": [
    "Component",
    "Container",
    "Container Instance",
    "Deployment Node",
    "Element",
    "Infrastructure Node",
    "Person",
    "Software System"
  ],
  "topLevel": [
    "customer",
    "administrator",
    "e-commerce-system",
    "payment-provider",
    "deploy/production/aws"
  ],
  "environments": [
    {
      "key": "production",
