docs.text:
• DSL API Reference - High-level DSL API (recommended)
  • Structurizr - the project that defines the Structurizr JSON schema
  • User Guide - Usage guide

docs.title: Use buildzr with AI agents
docs.text:
This guide shows how to give a coding agent, such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex, the buildzr skill, so that it can model your architecture, build it and answer questions about it.

A skill is a folder of instructions that a coding agent reads when a task needs it. The buildzr skill lives in the skills/buildzr folder of the buildzr repository, next to the code it describes, so each release of buildzr comes with a skill that matches it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • A coding agent that reads skills, in a project folder.
  • Node.js on the machine, to run the skills command with npx. Version 1.7.2 of skills asks for Node.js 22.20 or newer.
  • Python 3.10 or newer, and Node.js 18 or newer, for buildzr itself. The agent installs buildzr when it first needs it.

docs.title: Install the skill
docs.text:
In the folder of your project, run:

npx skills add amirulmenjeni/buildzr

The command finds the skill buildzr, asks which agents to install it for, and copies it into their folders, for example .claude/skills/buildzr/ for Claude Code. To choose without questions, name the skill and the agent:

npx skills add amirulmenjeni/buildzr --skill buildzr --agent claude-code -y

To see what the repository offers without installing anything, add --list.

docs.title: Install from a local checkout
docs.text:
To try the skill of a branch, or to work without network access to GitHub, give the path of a buildzr checkout instead of amirulmenjeni/buildzr:

npx skills add ../buildzr --list
npx skills add ../buildzr --skill buildzr --agent claude-code -y

docs.title: What the agent can do with the skill
docs.text:
With the skill installed, the agent:

  • installs buildzr and checks its version with buildzr --version;
  • writes model files in workspaces/: people, software systems, containers, components, relationships, groups, styles, and system landscape, system context, container, component, dynamic and deployment views;
  • runs buildzr build, reads the errors of a broken workspace, fixes the model file and builds again until the build passes;
  • starts buildzr serve and gives you the address of the viewer, or a link to one view or one element;
  • answers questions about a served workspace from its Model API, such as “what depends on the database?”, instead of reading the Python.

docs.title: Ask for a model
docs.text:
Give the agent a task in plain words. For example:

Model an online shop with buildzr: customers, a web app, an API, a database and a
payment provider. Produce a system context view, a container view and a deployment
view, and build it.

Expect the agent to create workspaces/<name>.py, run buildzr build until it prints a built .buildzr/build/<name> (...) line and exits with code 0, and tell you how to open the result with buildzr serve. The viewer shows all three views; the deployment view draws the servers or cloud services as nested boxes with the containers that run on them. If a build fails, the agent sees the same BROKEN block as you do (see When a workspace is broken) and fixes the file.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Let the agent, or any other program, query a served workspace: The Model API.
  • Learn the commands the agent runs: Command reference.
  • Read what the agent writes: Core Concepts and Views.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page shows how to install buildzr for each way of using it, and how to check the installation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • Node.js 18 or newer, only on the machine that builds: buildzr build, and buildzr serve when a workspace is new or changed. The layout step of the build runs elkjs on Node. Check your version with node --version. Serving workspaces that are already built (buildzr serve --no-build) and the Python API do not need Node.

buildzr supports every Python version that its CI (continuous integration) tests. New maintained Python versions are added when the dependencies support them. The oldest version is dropped only at its end of life, or when the tools make it impractical to keep.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
To add buildzr to a project that uses uv:

uv add buildzr

With pip instead: pip install buildzr. Both also install the buildzr command.

The right command depends on what you want to do:

You want to… Run Write models uv add buildzr (or pip install buildzr). Your model file imports buildzr, so buildzr must be in the environment of your project. Try the command line, or run it once, for example in CI uvx buildzr build. uvx runs buildzr in a temporary environment without installing it. uvx buildzr serve works the same way. Keep the buildzr command on your machine uv tool install buildzr

uvx buildzr build works without buildzr in your project. But when you run the model file yourself (python workspaces/model.py) or edit it in your editor, your project’s Python is used, and the import fails until you add buildzr to the project.

docs.title: Install a release candidate
docs.text:
A release candidate is a pre-release, such as 1.1.0rc1. A plain uv add buildzr or pip install buildzr never installs one; ask for it by version:

uvx --from buildzr==1.1.0rc1 buildzr build
uv add buildzr==1.1.0rc1
pip install buildzr==1.1.0rc1
pip install --pre buildzr

docs.title: buildzr[export-plantuml]
docs.text:
To export your diagrams to PlantUML, install the export-plantuml extra:

pip install "buildzr[export-plantuml]"

This extra needs Java 11 or newer, because it calls Structurizr’s Java libraries through JPype. To render svg or png, you also need Graphviz (dot), unless you pass layout='smetana'. See the Export page.

docs.title: Install from Source
docs.text:
To install the latest development version from the source code:

git clone https://github.com/amirulmenjeni/buildzr.git
cd buildzr
pip install -e .

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text:
For development work, install uv and sync the locked environment:

uv sync --all-extras --locked

This installs every extra, including the development, documentation and PlantUML extras. Run tools in the project environment with uv run, for example:

uv run pytest --mypy tests

The lock file uv.lock makes the dependencies of local development and of CI the same. To work on the documentation or to run the full test suite, use the devcontainer; see the Contributing Guide.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
To check your installation, import buildzr:

# no-run: checks the buildzr of your own environment
from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, SoftwareSystem, Person
print("buildzr installed successfully!")

Or print the installed version:

# no-run: checks the buildzr of your own environment
from importlib.metadata import version
print(version("buildzr"))

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: To create your first architecture diagram, continue with the Quick Start Guide. To serve several models, and let other people open them, continue with Serve your workspaces.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
In this tutorial, you describe a small software system in Python and open its diagram in your browser with buildzr serve, which builds the model and serves it in one step. At the end, you have a working model file and a diagram that you can click through.

Try it in your browser first

The complete example on this page has a Run Code button. It runs the model in your browser, without installing anything, and shows the model as JSON (the Structurizr workspace format). You do not need it for the tutorial.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • Node.js 18 or newer. The layout step of buildzr build runs on Node. Check your version with node --version.
  • uv, the Python package manager that this tutorial uses.

docs.title: 1. Create a project and install buildzr
docs.text:
Create a project folder, add buildzr to it, activate its virtual environment, and create a folder called workspaces:

uv init quickstart
cd quickstart
uv add buildzr
source .venv/bin/activate
mkdir workspaces

On Windows, activate the environment with .venv\Scripts\activate instead. The buildzr command is now available in this terminal.

The workspaces folder is where the buildzr command looks for your models. Each Python file in it describes one or more workspaces.

With pip, or without installing

With pip instead of uv: create and activate a virtual environment, then run pip install buildzr.

You can also run the commands of this tutorial without installing buildzr, by putting uvx in front of them (uvx buildzr serve). This tutorial installs buildzr anyway, because your editor needs it to understand the model file while you write it.

docs.title: 2. Start the model file
docs.text:
The model file is a Python file that describes your architecture. Create a file called hello.py in the workspaces folder, with this content:

# no-run: a step; the complete example at the end of the page runs
from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    pass

The first lines import what this tutorial uses from buildzr.dsl. Workspace holds your whole model: everything else in this tutorial goes inside the with block, in place of pass. Its name, hello, becomes part of the address at which you open the diagrams.

docs.title: 3. Add a person, a system and a relationship
docs.text:
Replace pass with a person, a software system, and a relationship between them. The new lines are highlighted:

# no-run: a step; the complete example at the end of the page runs
from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    user = Person('User', description='A user of the system')
    system = SoftwareSystem(
        'Web Application',
        description='Our main web application'
    )

    user >> "Uses" >> system

The line user >> "Uses" >> system says that the user uses the web application. “Uses” becomes the label of the arrow.

docs.title: 4. Give the person a person shape
docs.text:
Add a style that draws the user with the Person shape:

# no-run: a step; the complete example at the end of the page runs
from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    user = Person('User', description='A user of the system')
    system = SoftwareSystem(
        'Web Application',
        description='Our main web application'
    )

    user >> "Uses" >> system

    StyleElements(
        on=[user],
        shape='Person'
    )

docs.title: 5. Add a view
docs.text:
A view is a diagram that you choose to draw. Add a system context view of the web application: it shows the system and the people and systems around it.

# no-run: a step; the complete example at the end of the page runs
from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    user = Person('User', description='A user of the system')
    system = SoftwareSystem(
        'Web Application',
        description='Our main web application'
    )

    user >> "Uses" >> system

    StyleElements(
        on=[user],
        shape='Person'
    )

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=system,
        key='system-context',
        description='System Context View',
        auto_layout='tb'
    )

key='system-context' names the view; you use the name in a link in step 9. auto_layout='tb' asks Structurizr tools to lay the view out from top to bottom.

docs.title: 6. Compare your file with the complete example
docs.text:
Your workspaces/hello.py is now complete. It must look like this:

from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Person,
    StyleElements,
    SystemContextView,
)

with Workspace('hello') as w:
    user = Person('User', description='A user of the system')
    system = SoftwareSystem(
        'Web Application',
        description='Our main web application'
    )

    user >> "Uses" >> system

    StyleElements(
        on=[user],
        shape='Person'
    )

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=system,
        key='system-context',
        description='System Context View',
        auto_layout='tb'
    )

The file does not call w.save(). In the next step, buildzr serve runs the file and reads the workspace itself.

docs.title: 7. Build and serve the workspace
docs.text:
In the quickstart folder, start buildzr serve:

$ buildzr serve
built .buildzr/build/hello (2 elements, 1 relationship, 1 view; modelHash sha256:de1cb536d351…)
Serving .buildzr/build at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello/
Workspace list at http://127.0.0.1:8000/_buildzr/v1/workspaces

buildzr serve did two things:

  1. It built your workspace. It ran every Python file in workspaces, laid out the diagrams of the workspace that hello.py creates, and wrote the result to the folder .buildzr/build/hello: the web pages that draw your diagrams. The built line counts what your model contains: 2 elements (the user and the web application), 1 relationship and 1 view.
  2. It serves that folder at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. Each workspace has its own address, made from its name: /hello/.

The next time you start buildzr serve, it builds only the workspaces whose model file changed. It prints up to date: hello for the others.

docs.title: 8. Open the workspace in your browser
docs.text:
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in your browser. Because you have one workspace, the browser goes on to http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello/. You see the landscape: every person and software system of your model, like a System Landscape diagram of the C4 model. Here, that is the user, the web application and the “Uses” arrow between them.

The first screen. The left panel lists the elements of the model and, under Views, your System Context View.

Click the Web Application box. The right panel shows its details: its description, its path, the relationships that go in and out, and the views it appears in.

After the click. Under Incoming, the panel shows the “Uses” relationship from the User.

docs.title: 9. Open a link to one element
docs.text:
Every screen of the viewer has its own address. Open this address in your browser:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello/#/v/system-context?sel=user

The viewer opens the System Context View that you added in step 5, with the User selected. You can share such a link with anyone who can open the workspace.

The view opened from the link. The top bar shows View: System Context View, and the right panel shows the User.

To stop buildzr serve, press Ctrl+C in the terminal.

docs.title: 10. Build without serving
docs.text:
buildzr build does the first half of buildzr serve: it builds every workspace of the workspaces folder and stops. Use it when you want the built files only, for example to copy them to another machine:

$ buildzr build
built .buildzr/build/hello (2 elements, 1 relationship, 1 view; modelHash sha256:de1cb536d351…)

Unlike buildzr serve, buildzr build always builds every workspace again.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
You have written a model file, built it into a workspace and opened its diagrams. From here:

  • Learn how to describe more: Core Concepts, Models, Relationships and Views.
  • Serve several workspaces, and let other people open them: Serve your workspaces.
  • Look up every option of build, export and serve: Command reference.
  • Let scripts and AI assistants read your model as JSON: The Model API.

docs.title: Other ways to view the model
docs.text:
The viewer is the main way to view a buildzr model, but the model is also a standard Structurizr workspace in JSON. To write it to a file, run buildzr export workspaces/hello.py --pretty, which writes export/<workspace name>/workspace.json. Then you can open it with other tools:

  • Structurizr Lite shows the workspace in your browser. Run it in the folder that holds workspace.json (for example export/hello):

    docker run -it --rm -p 8080:8080 -v $PWD:/usr/local/structurizr structurizr/lite

  • Structurizr CLI converts the workspace to other formats, such as PlantUML and Mermaid.

  • PlantUML: buildzr export workspaces/hello.py -f plantuml -o output writes .puml files. It needs pip install "buildzr[export-plantuml]" and Java 11 or newer. Open the files with a C4-PlantUML viewer, for example the PlantUML web editor. See the Export page.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Think of architecture documentation as cartography for software. Just as maps use different scales — world atlas, country map, city guide, street view — software architecture needs multiple levels of detail to tell its story. buildzr helps you create these maps using a simple but powerful idea: zoom in progressively from the big picture to the fine details.

docs.title: The C4 Model: Architecture at Four Scales
docs.text:
buildzr is built around the C4 model, which provides a hierarchical approach to software architecture diagrams. The name “C4” comes from its four levels of abstraction:

Context → Containers → Components → Code

Think of it like Google Maps for your system:

  • Context: The 10,000-foot view. Who uses your system? What other systems does it talk to? This is the boardroom-friendly view that even your CEO can understand.
  • Containers: Zoom in to see the major technical building blocks — web apps, databases, mobile apps, microservices. Not Docker containers, but rather anything that runs or stores data.
  • Components: Zoom further to see how a container is internally structured — its major modules, packages, or meaningful groupings of functionality.
  • Code: The street-level view showing actual classes and interfaces. Often just UML diagrams (and honestly, you might not need this one unless you’re really into UML).

buildzr’s approach to building C4 Models is Models as Code, as opposed to just Diagrams as Code.

The brilliance of Models as Code is that you get to define your architecture model once, then create different views at different zoom levels for different audiences. You create different views to tell different stories about your software architectures, to work with different audiences, while using the same models.

docs.title: Workspace: Your Architecture Universe
docs.text:
A Workspace is where everything lives. It’s the top-level container for your entire architecture model — think of it as the canvas on which you’ll paint your system’s story.

A workspace contains three types of things:

  1. Models: The elements of your architecture (people, systems, containers, components) and how they relate
  2. Views: Different perspectives on those models — what you actually turn into diagrams
  3. Styles: Visual styling to make your diagrams readable and beautiful

The basic structure looks like this:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem, Container

with Workspace('my-architecture') as w:
    # Define your elements and relationships
    # Create views to visualize them
    # Apply styles to make them pretty
    ...

Check out Workspace for more info on Workspace.

docs.title: Elements: The Vocabulary of Architecture
docs.text: Architecture diagrams use a small vocabulary with big expressive power. There are just four core element types, each representing a different level of abstraction:

docs.title: Person
docs.text:
The humans (or bots pretending to be humans) who interact with your systems. Could be end users, administrators, or even external API clients represented as actors.

Example:

user = Person('Customer', description='Buys products from our store')

Learn more about defining people and other static models in the Models guide.

docs.title: Software System
docs.text:
The highest level of abstraction — a complete system that delivers value to its users. This is usually “your system” or one of the neighboring systems it talks to.

Example:

checkout = SoftwareSystem('Checkout System', description='Processes orders and payments')

See how software systems work in the Models guide.

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
A separately runnable or deployable unit within a software system. Web applications, mobile apps, databases, message queues — if it runs independently or stores data, it’s probably a container. (Yes, the name is confusing if you’re thinking Docker containers. Just roll with it.)

Example:

# no-run: a fragment; a container goes inside a software system
api = Container('REST API', technology='Python/FastAPI')

Dive into containers in the Models guide.

docs.title: Component
docs.text:
A grouping of related functionality within a container. Controllers, services, repositories — the major structural building blocks of your code.

Example: 

# no-run: a fragment; a component goes inside a container
auth = Component('Authentication Service', description='Handles login and tokens')

Explore components further in the Models guide.

docs.title: Relationships: The Conversations
docs.text:
Elements in isolation are just boxes. Relationships give them meaning — they show who talks to whom, what they’re saying, and how they’re saying it (REST API? Message queue? Smoke signals?).

The syntax is simple:

# no-run: the general form; source and destination stand for two elements
source >> "description" >> destination

You can add technical details, tags, properties, and handle complex scenarios like one-to-many relationships. The relationship system is flexible enough for real-world complexity while staying readable.

Example:

# no-run: a fragment; user, checkout_api and database are elements of your model
user >> "Places orders through" >> checkout_api
checkout_api >> ("Stores orders in", "JDBC") >> database

For a bit more in-depth guide on relationship, see Relationships.

docs.title: Groups: Organizing Chaos
docs.text:
As your architecture grows, you’ll want to organize related elements together. Groups let you cluster systems by team ownership, functional area, or any other logical grouping.

Example:

with Group("Internal Systems"): ...

Groups can nest, giving you as much organizational structure as you need. Learn more in the Workspace guide.

docs.title: Views: Choosing What to Show
docs.text:
Here’s where the magic happens. You’ve defined your architecture model — all the elements and their relationships. Now you create views to show different perspectives to different audiences.

Available view types:

  • System Landscape View: The complete organizational map — all systems and users
  • System Context View: One system and its immediate neighborhood
  • Container View: Zoom into a system to see its containers
  • Component View: Zoom into a container to see its components
  • Deployment View: Show where and how things run in production

Each view is a lens focused on a specific part of your model. You define your architecture once, then create multiple views to tell different parts of the story.

Example:

# no-run: a fragment; checkout is a software system of your model
SystemContextView(software_system_selector=checkout, key='checkout-context', description='Checkout and its users')

Learn more about views in Views.

docs.title: The Python Perspective
docs.text:
buildzr leverages Python’s context managers (with statements) to create hierarchical structures that mirror your architecture’s natural nesting:

with Workspace('e-commerce') as w:
    with SoftwareSystem('Shop') as shop:
        api = Container('API')
        with api:
            auth = Component('Auth Service')

This isn’t just syntactic sugar — it makes the code structure reflect the architecture structure. When you nest a container inside a system with a with block, you’re explicitly showing that containment relationship.

You can add tags and properties to categorize and annotate your architecture:

critical_system = SoftwareSystem(
    'Payment Processing',
    tags=['critical', 'pci-compliant'],
    properties={'Owner': 'Platform Team', 'SLA': '99.99%'}
)

Tags are particularly powerful when combined with styling — apply visual styles to all elements with a specific tag. See the Styling guide for details.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Workspace
  • Models
  • Relationships
  • Views

docs.title: Deployment Views
docs.text:
A deployment view shows where the containers of your model run: which cloud, which region, which cluster or server, and how many copies of each. This page shows how to write one, build it, and read it in the viewer.

You need a model with containers (see Models) and buildzr with its buildzr command (see Installation).

docs.title: 1. Write the deployment model
docs.text:
A deployment model has three parts:

  • a DeploymentEnvironment, such as Production or Staging;
  • DeploymentNodes inside it, nested as deep as you need: a cloud provider, a region, a cluster, a server;
  • ContainerInstances (or SoftwareSystemInstances) inside the nodes: the containers that run there. InfrastructureNodes are the other things on a node, such as a load balancer or a DNS service.

Save this as workspaces/shop.py:

from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem, Container,
    DeploymentEnvironment, DeploymentNode, InfrastructureNode, ContainerInstance,
    ContainerView, DeploymentView, StyleElements,
)

with Workspace('Shop Deployment') as w:
    customer = Person('Customer')
    with SoftwareSystem('Shop') as shop:
        api = Container('API', technology='Python, FastAPI', description='Takes orders')
        db = Container('Database', technology='PostgreSQL', tags={'Database'})
    customer >> ("Buys from", "HTTPS") >> api
    api >> ("Reads from and writes to", "SQL") >> db

    with DeploymentEnvironment('Production') as production:
        with DeploymentNode('AWS', technology='Amazon Web Services'):
            with DeploymentNode('eu-west-1', technology='AWS region'):
                lb = InfrastructureNode('Load Balancer', technology='Elastic Load Balancer')
                with DeploymentNode('ECS Cluster', technology='Amazon ECS', instances='2'):
                    api_instance = ContainerInstance(api)
                with DeploymentNode('RDS', technology='Amazon RDS'):
                    ContainerInstance(db)
                lb >> ("Forwards requests to", "HTTPS") >> api_instance

    ContainerView(software_system_selector=shop, key='shop-containers', description='The containers of the shop')
    DeploymentView(environment=production, key='production', software_system_selector=shop,
                   description='The shop in production')
    StyleElements(on=['Database'], shape='Cylinder')
  • instances='2' says the ECS Cluster runs two copies. It takes a number or a range such as '0..N'.
  • You do not write relationships between instances. The API container reads from the Database container, so buildzr gives the API instance the same relationship to the Database instance.
  • DeploymentView takes the environment object, not its name. software_system_selector limits the view to the instances of one software system; leave it out to show every instance of the environment.

docs.title: 2. Build and open the view
docs.text:
Build the workspace and serve it:

$ buildzr serve
built .buildzr/build/shop-deployment (11 elements, 3 relationships, 2 views; modelHash sha256:a464017ed5c8…)
Serving .buildzr/build at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/shop-deployment/
Workspace list at http://127.0.0.1:8000/_buildzr/v1/workspaces

The 11 elements are the person, the system, its two containers, and the seven deployment elements: four nodes, the load balancer and the two instances. Open the address and pick The shop in production under Views, or open http://127.0.0.1:8000/shop-deployment/#/v/production directly:

The deployment view of the Production environment. Each deployment node is a box around what runs on it, with its name and technology in the bottom-left corner.

What the view draws:

  • Deployment nodes are boxes around what runs on them, nested as in the model. A node with more than one instance has a badge in its top-right corner: ×2.
  • Instances look like the container they are an instance of: the same name, technology, description and style. The Database instance is a cylinder because the Database container has the tag Database.
  • Infrastructure nodes are boxes with [Infrastructure Node: <technology>].
  • Arrows are the relationships between the drawn elements. An arrow between two instances stands for the relationship between their containers.

A node with nothing inside it, no instance and no infrastructure node, is not in the view.

docs.title: 3. Select a node or an instance
docs.text:
Click a box to select it. The inspector on the right shows what the model says about it:

The ECS Cluster selected. The inspector shows its environment and its number of instances.

  • For a deployment node, the inspector shows the environment and the number of instances.
  • For an instance, it shows Instance of with a link to the container. Show in model opens the container in the model, where you can see what it is made of.
  • Search and the tag filter work in deployment views as in the other views: the matching boxes stay bright and the others are dimmed.

The model tree on the left lists the people, software systems, containers and components only. To reach a deployment element, open its deployment view or search for it.

docs.title: 4. Find where a container runs
docs.text:
Select a software system or a container in the model, and the inspector lists Deployed on: one line for each deployment instance of it, grouped by environment. Each line is the path of deployment nodes the instance sits in, with the number of copies of the innermost node when it is more than one (AWS › eu-west-1 › ECS Cluster ×3).

  • With one instance, the inspector has a Show deployment button. It opens the deployment view that draws the instance and selects the instance.
  • With several, the button reads Deployments (3) and moves you to the list. Pick a line to open its view. When the view you are in already draws the instance, the viewer stays in it.
  • With none, the list says “Not deployed in any environment.” and there is no button.
  • An instance that no deployment view draws is listed, but it is not a link: its line says “(in no deployment view)”. This happens when the environment has no DeploymentView, or when the view’s software_system_selector leaves the instance out.

The list only appears when the workspace has at least one DeploymentEnvironment. Back returns to the container, and the Instance of link in the inspector of an instance goes the other way. In an embedded viewer the same list works, and the history of the host page is not changed. On a phone, the button sits in the first lines of the sheet, and every line is at least 44 px high.

docs.title: 5. Link to a deployment element
docs.text:
Every deployment element has an id that starts with deploy/ and the environment: the ECS Cluster is deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster, and the API instance on it is deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster/api. An instance takes the name of its container.

To link to a selected element, add ?sel=<id> to the view’s address:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/shop-deployment/#/v/production?sel=deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster

The link #/m/<id> of a deployment element also works: it opens the first deployment view that shows the element. See Viewer links for every form of link.

docs.title: 6. On a phone
docs.text:
On a screen narrower than 768 px, the view fills the screen. Tap a box to select it; the inspector opens as a sheet at the bottom:

The same view on a phone, 390 px wide, with the ECS Cluster selected.

docs.title: 7. Ask the Model API
docs.text:
The Model API answers questions about deployment elements too. For example, this request lists the container instances and where they run (parent):

GET /shop-deployment/api/v1/elements?type=ContainerInstance

{
  "apiVersion": "1",
  "modelHash": "sha256:a464017ed5c8d6faffd1473e7f0653646c6c0b7d0522203cf1366b1ade2a23de",
  "total": 2,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster/api",
      "name": "API",
      "type": "ContainerInstance",
      "parent": "deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster",
      "description": "Takes orders",
      "technology": "Python, FastAPI",
      "tags": [
        "Container Instance"
      ],
      "childCount": 0,
      "viewerUrl": "/shop-deployment/#/v/production?sel=deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/ecs-cluster/api"
    },
    {
      "id": "deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/rds/database",
      "name": "Database",
      "type": "ContainerInstance",
      "parent": "deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/rds",
      "description": null,
      "technology": "PostgreSQL",
      "tags": [
        "Container Instance"
      ],
      "childCount": 0,
      "viewerUrl": "/shop-deployment/#/v/production?sel=deploy/production/aws/eu-west-1/rds/database"
    }
  ],
  "next": null,
  "truncated": false
}

GET /shop-deployment/api/v1/views?environment=production lists the deployment views of Production. See Deployment elements.

docs.title: Several environments
docs.text:
Write one DeploymentEnvironment per environment and one DeploymentView for each. Every environment gets its own ids: deploy/staging/... and deploy/production/.... Two environments whose names differ only in case or punctuation get -2 on the second one, for example deploy/prod-2/....

Deployment groups (DeploymentGroup) decide which instances get the relationships of their containers; the view does not draw them as boxes.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
A buildzr workspace can be exported as Structurizr JSON, or rendered through PlantUML as .puml source, SVG, or PNG. The way to do it is the buildzr export command. It runs a model file and writes every workspace the file creates, or the one you pick, so the model file does not need any export code.

Download an image from the viewer

The viewer can also save the diagram on screen as a PNG or SVG, in your browser, with its own layout and colours. See Download the diagram as an image. The command below draws with PlantUML instead.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Format Output json One Structurizr JSON file, workspace.json (default) plantuml One .puml file per view svg One .svg file per view (plus .puml) png One .png file per view (plus .puml) 
buildzr export workspaces/shop.py                      # export/shop/workspace.json
buildzr export workspaces/shop.py --pretty -o out      # indented JSON in out/
buildzr export workspaces/shop.py -f plantuml -f svg   # .puml and .svg files
buildzr export workspaces/shop.py -f png --layout smetana
buildzr export workspaces/many.py --workspace "Billing"   # one workspace of several

Every option is in the command reference. To get the content in memory instead of on disk (for example in a Jupyter notebook), use the methods of the workspace:

# no-run: needs Java for the PlantUML export, and the workspace w of your model
json_str = w.to_json()        # str
puml = w.to_plantuml()        # Dict[view_key, puml_source]
svg = w.to_svg()              # Dict[view_key, svg_source]; accepts layout=...

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Format Requirements json Nothing extra plantuml buildzr[export-plantuml] and Java 11+ svg, png As for plantuml, plus Graphviz dot on PATH (or set via GRAPHVIZ_DOT), unless you use --layout smetana

Install the extra with:

pip install "buildzr[export-plantuml]"

Graphviz is needed for the default layout engine. If GRAPHVIZ_DOT is set it must point to the dot executable; otherwise dot is looked up on PATH.

docs.title: Getting Java without root
docs.text:
If you cannot install Java system-wide, a version manager such as mise can provide it for a single command:

mise exec java@temurin-21 -- buildzr export model.py -f svg

docs.title: Output files and paths
docs.text:
buildzr export FILE -o DIR writes one subfolder of DIR (default export) for each workspace, named after the workspace: Workspace('Big Bank plc') is written to DIR/big-bank-plc/. Two workspaces with the same name get -2, -3 and so on. In the subfolder:

  • workspace.json is the JSON.
  • Each view is written as <view key>.<ext>.
  • svg and png also write the .puml source next to each image.

docs.title: Migrating from Workspace.save()
docs.text:
Workspace.save() is deprecated. It still works exactly as before and returns the same values, but it emits a DeprecationWarning that points here, and it will be removed in a future release. A model file that still calls it can be exported with buildzr export unchanged: the command runs the file in a temporary folder and silences this warning, so nothing is written next to your model.

Before After w.save(path='workspace.json') buildzr export model.py -o out (writes out/<name>/workspace.json) w.save(path='workspace.json', pretty=True) buildzr export model.py --pretty w.save(format='plantuml', path='d/') buildzr export model.py -f plantuml -o d w.save(format='svg', path='d/', layout='smetana') buildzr export model.py -f svg --layout smetana -o d w.save(format='png', path='d/') buildzr export model.py -f png -o d

Differences to know:

  • The files go into a subfolder per workspace, workspace.json and <view key>.<ext> inside it, so a file that creates several workspaces does not overwrite itself. save() took the file or folder you gave it.
  • Delete the w.save(...) line from the model file when you can. A file without it also works with buildzr build and buildzr serve.
  • If you need the content in a program, to_json(), to_plantuml() and to_svg() are not deprecated.
  • To silence the warning while you migrate, use warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message=r"Workspace\.save\(\) is deprecated", category=DeprecationWarning).

docs.title: Rendering without Graphviz
docs.text:
Pass --layout smetana to use PlantUML’s built-in Java port of Graphviz instead of the dot executable:

buildzr export workspaces/shop.py -f svg --layout smetana -o diagrams

In Python, w.to_svg(layout='smetana') does the same in memory.

Java is still required. The trade-off is that the layout quality is somewhat worse than with dot. With --layout smetana, the line !pragma layout smetana is also written into the generated .puml files, so they match the images. to_plantuml() takes no layout argument.

docs.title: Failure behaviour
docs.text:
buildzr export prints buildzr: error: ... and exits with 1 when something fails, and with 2 when the file, --workspace or --index is wrong (see the exit codes).

  • If jpype1 is not installed, plantuml, svg and png fail with the install hint above.
  • If Graphviz is missing (with the default dot layout), the error says so and suggests --layout smetana. These two checks run before any file is written, so a run that asks for json and svg writes nothing when Graphviz is missing.
  • If PlantUML reports an error instead of producing a diagram, the error is printed and the exit status is 1.
  • -f plantuml never needs Graphviz.

In Python, the same problems raise ImportError and PlantUmlRenderError (a subclass of RuntimeError) from to_plantuml() and to_svg():

# no-run: needs Java for the PlantUML export, and the workspace w of your model
from buildzr.sinks.plantuml_sink import PlantUmlRenderError

try:
    svgs = w.to_svg()
except PlantUmlRenderError as e:
    print(f"Rendering failed: {e}")

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Models are the fundamental building blocks of your architecture documentation in buildzr. They represent the different elements that make up your software system, from high-level abstractions like people and systems down to specific implementation details like components and deployment infrastructure. buildzr provides full support for all core C4 model element types, enabling you to create comprehensive architecture diagrams at multiple levels of detail.

docs.title: Understanding Model Categories
docs.text:
Your architecture models can be divided into two distinct categories: static models and instance models.

Static models define the logical architecture of your system — the abstract concepts, relationships, and structure of your software independent of any specific deployment. These include people who interact with the system, the software systems themselves, and their internal structure broken down into containers and components. Static models answer questions like “What systems exist?” and “How are they organized?”

Instance models describe the physical deployment and runtime manifestation of your static models. They represent where and how your software actually runs in the real world — deployment environments, infrastructure nodes, and specific instances of containers deployed to those nodes. Instance models answer questions like “Where does this run?” and “What infrastructure supports it?”

This separation allows you to define your architecture once as static models, then map those same containers and systems to different deployment scenarios (development, staging, production) without duplicating the core architectural definitions.

Static models:

  • Person
  • SoftwareSystem
  • Container
  • Component
  • Element (custom element, outside C4 model)

Instance models:

  • DeploymentEnvironment
  • DeploymentNode
  • SoftwareSystemInstance
  • ContainerInstance
  • InfrastructureNode

To walk you through the models, let’s use Structurizr’s Amazon Web Services example.

docs.title: Person
docs.text:
Person represents human users, actors, roles, or personas.

user = Person("User", description="An ordinary user.")

docs.title: Software System
docs.text:
SoftwareSystem represents the highest level of abstraction. A software system may contain zero or more containers.

with SoftwareSystem('Online Shop') as shop:
    # Its containers goes here.
    ...

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
Container represents an application, data store, or service within a software system. A container may contain zero or more components.

Here, we define the containers inside the software system shop we’ve defined above.

with SoftwareSystem("Online Shop") as shop:

    wa = Container("Web Application", technology="Java and Spring boot")

    db = Container("Database Schema")

    wa >> "Reads from and writes to" >> db

Notice that we’ve also described a relationship between the web application wa and the database db of the software system shop.

docs.title: Component
docs.text:
Component represents a component within a container.

The wa web application may further be comprised of several layers, each serving different purpose. For example, in an Onion Architecture, your web application might have an API layer that listens for HTTP requests, which may in turn run queries or transactions via the database layer.

with SoftwareSystem("Online Shop") as shop:

    wa = Container("Web Application", technology="Java and Spring boot")

    db = Container("Database Schema")

    wa >> "Reads from and writes to" >> db

    with wa:
        api_layer = Component("API Layer")
        db_layer = Component("Database Layer")

        api_layer >> "Runs queries/transactions on" >> db_layer

docs.title: Custom Element
docs.text:
Element represents a custom element that sits outside the C4 model. Custom elements are useful when you need to model things that don’t fit neatly into the Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, or Component hierarchy — for example, hardware devices, business processes, non-software entities, or abstract concepts.

Schema Note

buildzr’s JSON output is derived from the Structurizr JSON schema of Structurizr. The official Structurizr JSON schema does not include customElements or customViews fields. However, the Structurizr CLI and DSL fully support these features. The buildzr implementation is based on testing with structurizr.sh export to discover the actual JSON structure used at runtime.

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Element, CustomView

with Workspace('Hardware Architecture') as w:
    # focus: view:hardware-view
    # Custom elements for non-C4 architecture
    controller = Element(
        "Hardware Controller",
        metadata="Hardware",
        description="Main controller unit",
        tags={"embedded", "critical"},
        properties={"vendor": "Acme Corp"}
    )

    sensor = Element("Temperature Sensor", metadata="Hardware")
    actuator = Element("Motor Actuator", metadata="Hardware")

    # Relationships between custom elements
    sensor >> "sends data to" >> controller
    controller >> "controls" >> actuator

    # A CustomView shows the custom elements and their relationships
    CustomView(
        key="hardware-view",
        description="Hardware component interactions",
    )

Custom elements can have relationships with C4 elements (Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component) and can be displayed in any view type — including SystemLandscapeView, SystemContextView, and CustomView. The web viewer lists them after the C4 elements in its model tree and draws them in the views that include them; see Custom elements in the web viewer.

docs.title: Element Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description name str The name of the custom element (required) metadata str Metadata/type label for the element (e.g., “Hardware”, “Process”) description str A short description of the element tags Set[str] Tags for styling and filtering properties Dict[str, Any] Arbitrary key-value properties

docs.title: Properties and Metadata
docs.text:
You can add properties to enrich your models with metadata.

system = SoftwareSystem(
    'System',
    properties={
        'Owner': 'Platform Team',
        'Cost Center': 'IT-001',
        'SLA': '99.9%'
    }
)

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Models can also be assigned tags.

critical_system = SoftwareSystem(
    'Payment System',
    tags=['critical', 'pci-compliant', 'monitored']
)

In Structurizr, the purpose of tags are used primarily for styling and visual representation of elements. For example, if an element is tagged as critical, you can apply a specific style (e.g., red colored background) to all elements tagged as critical.

buildzr offer a more flexible styling syntax beyond tagging. See Styles.

Note

If you run the code above, you will see that the critical_system has some extra additional “hidden” tags: Element and SoftwareSystem. By default, each model element will have default tags assigned to them: the model type (Relationship or Element) and, if it’s an Element, the type of the element (e.g., SoftwareSystem, Person, Container, or Component).

docs.title: Deployment Elements
docs.text: Now that we’ve defined the static models, let’s detail out our architecture further by modeling how they’re meant to be run or hosted.

docs.title: Deployment Environment
docs.text:
DeploymentEnvironment defines a deployment context (e.g., Development, Staging, Production). Each environment can have its own set of deployment nodes and infrastructure.

with DeploymentEnvironment('Production') as prod:
    # Define deployment nodes
    pass

docs.title: Deployment Node
docs.text:
DeploymentNode represents infrastructure or runtime environment where your containers are deployed. Deployment nodes can be nested to represent hierarchical infrastructure (e.g., cloud provider → region → cluster → instance).

with SoftwareSystem('Web Application') as system:
    api = Container(
        'API',
        description='Provides REST API',
        technology='Python/FastAPI'
    )

with DeploymentEnvironment('Production') as prod:
    with DeploymentNode('AWS'):
        with DeploymentNode('EC2', technology='Ubuntu 22.04'):
            # Deploy containers
            api_instance = ContainerInstance(api)

docs.title: Infrastructure Node
docs.text:
InfrastructureNode represents supporting infrastructure components that don’t host containers but are essential to your system (load balancers, message queues, caches, etc.).

with DeploymentNode('AWS'):
    load_balancer = InfrastructureNode(
        'Load Balancer',
        description='Distributes traffic',
        technology='AWS ELB'
    )

docs.title: Deployment Group
docs.text:
DeploymentGroup allows us to group deployment instances together so relationships only exist between instances sharing the same deployment group, enabling isolated multi-instance deployments like multi-tenant or blue-green scenarios.

In this example, we’ll use DeploymentGroup to isolate instance relationships within their respective region (ap-southeast-1 and us-east-1).

with Workspace(
    "Amazon Web Services Example",
    description="An example AWS deployment architecture",
) as w:

    user = Person("User", description="An ordinary user.")

    with SoftwareSystem("Online Shop") as shop:

        # Notice that we don't need to specify the tags "Application" and "Database"
        # for styling -- just pass the `wa` and `db` variables directly to the `StyleElements` class.
        wa = Container("Web Application", technology="Java and Spring boot")
        db = Container("Database Schema")

        wa >> "Reads from and writes to" >> db

        with wa:
            api_layer = Component("API Layer")
            db_layer = Component("Database Layer")

            api_layer >> "Runs queries/transactions on" >> db_layer

    user >> ("Uses", "browser") >> shop

    with DeploymentEnvironment("Live") as live:

        dg_region_1 = DeploymentGroup("region-1")
        dg_region_2 = DeploymentGroup("region-2")

        with DeploymentNode("Amazon Web Services") as aws:
            aws.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Cloud")

            with DeploymentNode("ap-southeast-1") as region_ap_southeast_1:
                region_ap_southeast_1.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Region")

                dns = InfrastructureNode(
                    "DNS Router",
                    description="Routes incoming requests based upon domain name.",
                    technology="Route 53",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Route 53"}
                )

                lb = InfrastructureNode(
                    "Load Balancer",
                    description="Automatically distributes incoming application traffic.",
                    technology="Elastic Load Balancer",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Elastic Load Balancing"}
                )

                dns >> ("Fowards requests to", "HTTP") >> lb

                with DeploymentNode("Autoscaling Group", tags={"Amazon Web Services - Auto Scaling"}) as asg:
                    with DeploymentNode("Amazon EC2 - Ubuntu Server", tags={"Amazon Web Services - EC2 Instance"}):
                        lb >> "Forwards requests to" >> ContainerInstance(wa, deployment_groups=[dg_region_1])

                with DeploymentNode("Amazon RDS", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS"}) as rds:
                    with DeploymentNode("MySQL", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS MySQL instance"}):
                        database_instance = ContainerInstance(db, deployment_groups=[dg_region_1])

            with DeploymentNode("us-east-1") as region_us_east_1:
                region_us_east_1.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Region")

                dns = InfrastructureNode(
                    "DNS Router",
                    description="Routes incoming requests based upon domain name.",
                    technology="Route 53",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Route 53"}
                )

                lb = InfrastructureNode(
                    "Load Balancer",
                    description="Automatically distributes incoming application traffic.",
                    technology="Elastic Load Balancer",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Elastic Load Balancing"}
                )

                dns >> ("Fowards requests to", "HTTP") >> lb

                with DeploymentNode("Autoscaling Group", tags={"Amazon Web Services - Auto Scaling"}) as asg:
                    with DeploymentNode("Amazon EC2 - Ubuntu Server", tags={"Amazon Web Services - EC2 Instance"}):
                        lb >> "Forwards requests to" >> ContainerInstance(wa, deployment_groups=[dg_region_2])

                with DeploymentNode("Amazon RDS", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS"}) as rds:
                    with DeploymentNode("MySQL", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS MySQL instance"}):
                        database_instance = ContainerInstance(db, deployment_groups=[dg_region_2])

Deployment Groups Use Case

In this example, DeploymentGroup ensures that the web app on ap-southeast-1 (with deployment group region-1) only connects to the database in the same region. Likewise, the deployment group region-2 ensures that the web app in us-east-1 region only connects to the database in the same region.

In effect, DeploymentGroup allows us to specify the relationship boundary of SoftwareInstances or ContainerInstances.

Without specifying DeploymentGroup, SoftwareInstances or ContainerInstances will share the same default deployment group. Since all instances across all regions share the same default deployment group, the web app in the first region would look like it is connecting to the database in the second region, and vice versa. Which is not something we’d want.

Without deployment group, we’d have something like this (rendered with PlantUML):

However, if we specify the deployment group like we did in the example above, we avoid drawing a relationship between instances across the region:

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
Note

We’ve added a SystemContextView and a DeploymentView in the code below, so that the model has diagrams to show. To see them, build and serve the file with buildzr build and buildzr serve, as the Quick Start shows. The viewer draws the deployment view with the AWS regions and nodes as nested boxes around the containers that run on them; Deployment Views shows how to read it.

So far, we’ve only discussed models. With views, we can use (and re-use!) our static and instance models to draw architecture diagrams. See Views for more info.

from buildzr.dsl import (
    Workspace,
    Person,
    SoftwareSystem,
    Container,
    Component,
    DeploymentEnvironment,
    DeploymentGroup,
    DeploymentNode,
    InfrastructureNode,
    ContainerInstance,
    SystemContextView,
    DeploymentView,
    StyleElements,
)

with Workspace(
    "Amazon Web Services Example",
    description="An example AWS deployment architecture",
) as w:

    user = Person("User", description="An ordinary user.")

    with SoftwareSystem("Online Shop") as shop:

        # Notice that we don't need to specify the tags "Application" and "Database"
        # for styling -- just pass the `wa` and `db` variables directly to the `StyleElements` class.
        wa = Container("Web Application", technology="Java and Spring boot")
        db = Container("Database Schema")

        wa >> "Reads from and writes to" >> db

        with wa:
            api_layer = Component("API Layer")
            db_layer = Component("Database Layer")

            api_layer >> "Runs queries/transactions on" >> db_layer

    user >> ("Uses", "browser") >> shop

    with DeploymentEnvironment("Live") as live:

        dg_region_1 = DeploymentGroup("region-1")
        dg_region_2 = DeploymentGroup("region-2")

        with DeploymentNode("Amazon Web Services") as aws:
            aws.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Cloud")

            with DeploymentNode("ap-southeast-1") as region_ap_southeast_1:
                region_ap_southeast_1.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Region")

                dns = InfrastructureNode(
                    "DNS Router",
                    description="Routes incoming requests based upon domain name.",
                    technology="Route 53",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Route 53"}
                )

                lb = InfrastructureNode(
                    "Load Balancer",
                    description="Automatically distributes incoming application traffic.",
                    technology="Elastic Load Balancer",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Elastic Load Balancing"}
                )

                dns >> ("Fowards requests to", "HTTP") >> lb

                with DeploymentNode("Autoscaling Group", tags={"Amazon Web Services - Auto Scaling"}) as asg:
                    with DeploymentNode("Amazon EC2 - Ubuntu Server", tags={"Amazon Web Services - EC2 Instance"}):
                        lb >> "Forwards requests to" >> ContainerInstance(wa, deployment_groups=[dg_region_1])

                with DeploymentNode("Amazon RDS", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS"}) as rds:
                    with DeploymentNode("MySQL", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS MySQL instance"}):
                        database_instance = ContainerInstance(db, deployment_groups=[dg_region_1])

            with DeploymentNode("us-east-1") as region_us_east_1:
                region_us_east_1.add_tags("Amazon Web Services - Region")

                dns = InfrastructureNode(
                    "DNS Router",
                    description="Routes incoming requests based upon domain name.",
                    technology="Route 53",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Route 53"}
                )

                lb = InfrastructureNode(
                    "Load Balancer",
                    description="Automatically distributes incoming application traffic.",
                    technology="Elastic Load Balancer",
                    tags={"Amazon Web Services - Elastic Load Balancing"}
                )

                dns >> ("Fowards requests to", "HTTP") >> lb

                with DeploymentNode("Autoscaling Group", tags={"Amazon Web Services - Auto Scaling"}) as asg:
                    with DeploymentNode("Amazon EC2 - Ubuntu Server", tags={"Amazon Web Services - EC2 Instance"}):
                        lb >> "Forwards requests to" >> ContainerInstance(wa, deployment_groups=[dg_region_2])

                with DeploymentNode("Amazon RDS", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS"}) as rds:
                    with DeploymentNode("MySQL", tags={"Amazon Web Services - RDS MySQL instance"}):
                        database_instance = ContainerInstance(db, deployment_groups=[dg_region_2])

    SystemContextView(
        software_system_selector=shop,
        key='online_shop_context_00',
        description="System context of Online Shop",
    )

    DeploymentView(
        environment=live,
        key='aws-deployment-view',
        software_system_selector=shop,
        title="Amazon Web Services Deployment",
        description="Deployment view of the web application on AWS",
        auto_layout='lr',
    )

    StyleElements(on=['Element'], background='#ffffff')
    StyleElements(on=['Container'], background='#ffffff')
    StyleElements(on=[wa], background='#ffffff')
    StyleElements(on=[user], shape='Person')
    StyleElements(on=[db], shape='Cylinder')

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: Relationships connect elements in your architecture model and describe how they interact and work together to bring value. Without relationships, your architecture diagrams aren’t really helpful. With that in mind, let’s dive into how we can establish and maintain a healthy relationship with buildzr.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
To define a relationship between two models, use the >> operator.

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace('w') as w:

    user = Person('User')
    system = SoftwareSystem('System')

    # Simple relationship
    user >> system

docs.title: Adding Descriptions
docs.text:
To describe what kind of relationship exists between user and system, simply pass a string like so:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem

with Workspace('w') as w:

    user = Person('User')
    system = SoftwareSystem('System')

    user >> "Uses" >> system

docs.title: Technology/Protocol
docs.text:
If you need to add the technology detail, pass a tuple instead of a string. The first element of the tuple is the description, while the second is the technology.

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, SoftwareSystem, Container

with Workspace('w') as w:

    with SoftwareSystem('s') as s:
        api = Container('API')
        database = Container('Database')

    # Relationship with description and technology
    api >> ("Reads from and writes to", "JDBC/SSL") >> database

docs.title: Adding Tags and Properties to a Relationship
docs.text:
Like element models, you can also add tags and properties to relationships by piping (|) the relationship to a With:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, SoftwareSystem, Container, With

with Workspace('w') as w:

    with SoftwareSystem('s') as s:
        api = Container('API')
        database = Container('Database')

    # Relationship with description and technology
    api >> ("Reads from and writes to", "JDBC/SSL") >> database | With(
        tags={'sensitive'},
        properties={
            'driver': 'mysql-connector-java-5.1.18-bin.jar',
        }
    )

docs.title: One-to-Many Relationships
docs.text:
It is also possible to define a one-to-many relationships by collecting the right-hand hand side of the >> in a list ([ ... ]):

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem, With, desc

with Workspace('w') as w:
    user = Person('user')
    system_a = SoftwareSystem('a')
    system_b = SoftwareSystem('b')
    auth_system = SoftwareSystem('auth')

    user >> [
        desc("Reads from") >> system_a,
        desc("Writes to", "HTTPS") >> system_b | With(
            tags={'encrypted'},
        ),
        auth_system,
    ]

You can see that we’ve combined different ways to define a relationship for each relationship between user and system_a, system_b, and auth_system!

Note

Use desc when describing relationships in a one-to-many relationships definition. This is required, unless you don’t need to put a relationship description like with auth_system above!

docs.title: Bidirectional Relationships
docs.text:
Sometimes relationships go both ways. When system A talks to system B and system B talks back to system A, you’ve got a bidirectional relationship.

You can create relationships in both directions by defining each direction separately:

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem, With, desc

with Workspace('w') as w:
    system_a = SoftwareSystem('a')
    system_b = SoftwareSystem('b')

    system_a >> "Calls" >> system_b

    system_b >> "Sends events to" >> system_a

Tip

Just because you can make relationships bidirectional doesn’t mean they are. Only add the reverse relationship if it actually exists in your system.

For example, if there’s a “data flow” from system A to system B, ask yourself (or your fellow architects): Is system A calling a procedure to system B to upload/ingest the data into system B? Or is system B running a query against system A? The latter relationship is not the same as the former!

docs.title: Implied Relationships
docs.text:
Sometimes you don’t need to say the obvious. If your frontend container talks to someone else’s api container, it’s pretty clear that your system talks to their system too. These are implied relationships - connections that exist by logical necessity, not because you explicitly wrote them down.

from buildzr.dsl import Workspace, Person, SoftwareSystem, Container

# ⚠️ Make sure to enable `implied_relationships` for the workspace!
with Workspace('w', implied_relationships=True) as w:
    user = Person('user')
    with SoftwareSystem('s') as s:
        app = Container('app')

    # This will also imply that `user >> s`.
    user >> app

If you run the code above and inspect the JSON output, you’ll see that user has two relationships:

  • The first one with app, which was explicitly created, and
  • The second one with s, which was implied

Why This Matters

Implied relationships save you from maintaining duplicate relationship definitions across different abstraction levels. Define the detailed container-to-container relationship once, and the system-to-system relationship is inferred automatically.

Implied Relationships are Bidirectional

If we have software systems a and b, each with containers ca and cb respectively, the following holds: - a.ca >> b implies a >> b - a >> b.cb implies a >> b

docs.title: Legal Relationships
docs.text:
As you may know, not all relationships are legal.

buildzr helps you know if you’re creating a legal relationship by using Mypy, a static type checker for Python.

For example, if you try to create a relationship between a Person and an DeploymentNode (ew!), Mypy will complain:

# no-run: wrong on purpose: Mypy rejects this relationship
with Workspace('w') as w:
    user = Person('user')
    region = DeploymentNode('region')
    user >> region # Illegal: Mypy will complain!

Mypy complaints will read something like this:

No overload variant of "__rshift__" of "DslElementRelationOverrides" matches argument type "DeploymentNode".

Possible overload variants:
    def __rshift__(self, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component], /) -> _Relationship[Person, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]
    def __rshift__(self, Tuple[str, str], /) -> _UsesFrom[Person, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]
    def __rshift__(self, str, /) -> _UsesFrom[Person, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]
    def __rshift__(self, _RelationshipDescription[Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]], /) -> _UsesFrom[Person, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]
    def __rshift__(self, List[Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component, _UsesFromLate[Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]]], /) -> List[_Relationship[Person, Union[Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component]]]

The following table shows the allowed relationships between which element types, and from which source to which destination (taken from Structurizr DSL Language Reference):

Source Destination Person Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component SoftwareSystem Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component Container Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component Component Person, SoftwareSystem, Container, Component DeploymentNode DeploymentNode InfrastructureNode DeploymentNode, InfrastructureNode, SoftwareSystemInstance, ContainerInstance SoftwareSystemInstance InfrastructureNode ContainerInstance InfrastructureNode

Note that the table shows that SoftwareSystemInstance and ContainerInstance can only have a relationship with InfrastructureNode. Behind the scene, though, when you create a relationship, say, between two Containers, buildzr will create the implied instance relationships between the instances of the two ContainerInstances if they exists. For an example of this, see the Deployment Group example. (This is a different feature, not to be confused with from what’s described in Implied Relationships.)
